subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he can give the house a report on the present situation in Cyprus, particularly whether in the last day or so there have been any signs that the situation is alleviating.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation in Cyprus is that the government of Turkey has relented in respect of a position it had announced it was going to take with regard to the sending of supplies to the island, an act that was thought to contain elements of provocation. The decision now is that the Turkish government, in response to an appeal by the United Nations secretary general to postpone the sending of the shipment, has agreed to do so if the United Nations will provide the necessary arrangements for further food shipments to reach Kokkina. Arrangements are being made to this end.
This has considerably eased the situation. As the right hon. gentleman knows, the secretary general has circulated a report with regard to the operation of the force, and this will be considered by the security council on Thursday, I think.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Would the minister say whether there has been any agreement on the part of Canada to continue its force in Cyprus indefinitely, or whether a limitation has been placed on the availability of the Canadian force?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
There has been no decision by the Canadian government to contribute forces indefinitely, nor has there been any decision reached as to further participation in the force. I would not want this last remark to be interpreted as meaning that, given the necessary conditions, we would not continue to live up to our obligations under the charter. The security council 20220-508
is meeting, and after that meeting has taken place I fully expect that the secretary general will get in touch with the participating governments.

subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE    APPROVAL OF RATIFICATION OF COLUMBIA RIVER TREATY
MR. HERRIDGE    APPROVAL OF RATIFICATION OF COLUMBIA RIVER TREATY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all hon. members of the house, and a most important question of privilege of national and international consequence, which is evident from a page I have just received taken from the Spokesman-Review of Spokane of Friday, September 11 in which there appeared an editorial entitled "Canada's Pearson Campaigns for L. B. J.".
It goes on to say:
-Mr. Johnson's long lasso has roped him into domestic political affairs in the United Statesand calls it a wholly unnecessary expedition at this time. It adds:
It is unfortunate that Prime Minister Pearson -who has plenty of domestic troubles of his own -is now being dragged into the American political campaignand says it is:
-a low-level political blow at. ..many northwest citizensand so on. I mention that editorial to indicate the international as well as the national significance of my point of privilege. The question concerns the apparent misinterpretation by ministers of the crown of a resolution of this house.
As this misinterpretation may have misleading consequences in our treaty relations with the United States of America and our domestic relations with the province of British Columbia, I believe this house must clarify the constitutional meaning and limits of that resolution to the end that those members of this house who, as advisers to His Excellency the Governor General, must aid and assist His Excellency in implementing that resolution, do not construe the resolution as a licence to arrogate and usurp to themselves, without counselling with His Excellency, the statutory prerogative of his excellency the governor general in council in matters of disallowance.
Such misinterpretation is implicit in the announcement by the Prime Minister of his intended participation in an international ceremony to celebrate the purported coming into force of the treaty.
20220-508J
Question of Privilege
1.	The resolution of the house approving the ratification of the Columbia treaty, so-called, with the protocol and exchange of notes, as recorded in the Journals of the house for June 5, 1964, is subject to section 90 of the B.N.A. Act with respect to the disallowance of a provincial statute.
2.	Article XIV (1) of the treaty requires
that Canada designate a Canadian entity for the purpose of the treaty. The note of January 22,	1964, with the attachment thereto,
provides in article C that Canada shall designate the British Columbia hydro and power authority as the Canadian entity for the purpose of article XIV (1). The designation of that authority is therefore incorporated by reference in the treaty, and, as so incorporated, was approved in the resolution of this house.
3.	The British Columbia hydro and power authority was established under the provisions of an act, cited as the British Columbia hydro and power authority act, 1964, passed by the legislature of British Columbia on or about March 10, 1964.
4.	Some time after March 10, 1964 a copy of the act was forwarded to the Governor General of Canada by the lieutenant governor of British Columbia.
5.	Under section 90 of the B.N.A. Act, the governor in council may disallow the act within one year of the receipt of the act by the Governor General.
6.	On March 16, 1960 Mr. Speaker ruled that the question of disallowance is a power which has been entrusted to the exectuive and not to parliament. Therefore it follows from this Speaker's decision that the approval of the house of June 5, 1964 to the treaty, protocol and notes, and in particular to article XIV (1) as incorporating by reference the designation of the British Columbia hydro and power authority in article C of the attachment to the note of January 22, 1964, was and is subject to the exercise or nonexercise by the executive of its power to annul the provincial statute that creates the British Columbia hydro and power authority. In other words-

subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE    APPROVAL OF RATIFICATION OF COLUMBIA RIVER TREATY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE    APPROVAL OF RATIFICATION OF COLUMBIA RIVER TREATY
speechtext:
I am glad I am getting applause, because I worked very hard on this question of privilege.
In other words, unless the governor in council sooner disallows the British Columbia statute, then the approval of the house to the treaty is in effect in escrow for one

Question of Privilege
year after the receipt by the Governor General of a copy of the British Columbia act. Putting the matter another way, under section 90 of the British North America Act the executive may disallow the British Columbia act within one year, but there is no positive way by which the governor in council can indicate that it, or a successor governor in council, will not disallow the act. The governor in council can only approve the act by letting one year elapse without disallowing the act.
The matter is put neatly in the question of the member for Vancouver East and the reply of Mr. Speaker thereto in the course of the Speaker's decision already cited, as it appears in Hansard for March 16, 1960, volume II at page 2121:

subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE    APPROVAL OF RATIFICATION OF COLUMBIA RIVER TREATY
speechtext: That is the very point. Do I understand from what you have just said that the House of Commons cannot deal with this matter until the last minute of the period of authority of the cabinet to deal with the matter; and, if so, that we cannot even raise it then because by that time the time has expired and it is a fait accompli? Is that the case?

subtopic: MR. HERRIDGE    APPROVAL OF RATIFICATION OF COLUMBIA RIVER TREATY
speechtext:
That is precisely the situation-
Applying the principle of that ruling to this case, the ratification by this house of the treaty is not effective until the last minute of authority of the governor in council to deal with the matter. Under our constitution the ratification by this house is either valid or invalid depending upon:
(a)	The elapse of one year from some time in the spring of 1964 without the governor in council disallowing the British Columbia hydro and power authority act, 1964; or
(b)	the disallowance of the act by the governor in council within that year with the consequential nullification of the ratification by this house.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowiehan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron):
That the resolution of this house of the 5th June 1964 concerning the approval of the ratification of the Columbia river treaty, so called, in no way derogates from or impinges upon the powers and authorities conferred upon and entrusted to the governor general in council under section 90 of the British North America Act relating to the disallowance of an act entitled the British Columbia hydro and power authority act, 1964 as passed by the legislature of the province of British Columbia.
And therefore, to quieten doubts that have arisen or may arise as to the interpretation and effect of the said resolution, be it recorded in the Journal of this house that this house declares that the said resolution is subject to and dependant upon the powers and authorities so conferred upon and entrusted to his excellency the governor general in council.
[Mr. Herridge.l

Hon. Arihur Laing (Minister of Northern
Affairs and National Resources): Mr. Speaker,
I will first of all disappoint the hon. member by telling him that I have no intention of resigning. This is an advisory body. In the past we have thought that in these unorganized areas within our parks such bodies were good things. After the decision taken last evening I am going to be more cautious about the advice I accept from that particular body.
Two of the reasons given for the action were that we were running contrary to the Oberlander report, and were running contrary to recommendations of the land use code. speechtext: I do not feel it my duty to make any statement on my personal reaction to the performance of the Beatles, or to draw any inferences from comparisons with other people. maintopic: CHANGE IN ORDER OP BUSINESS FOR TODAY

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CHANGE IN ORDER OP BUSINESS FOR TODAY
speechtext:
Before the first item of business is called I think I owe it to the house to advise hon. members of a slight change which will take place in the order of business as announced last evening.
I had announced that we would first proceed with the second reading and committee stage of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, after which we would take the resolution preceding the bill relating to the Crop Insurance Act, to be followed by the resolution preceding the bill with respect to farm machinery syndicates. The order in which these last two resolutions will be taken will be inverted, and after the committee stage of the Farm Improvement Loans Act I will ask the clerk to call the resolution in respect to the farm machinery syndicates.
In view of certain circumstances which have been explained to the leaders of the other parties, I wish to advise the house that I propose, if we get through the committee stage of the farm loans act today, to ask for agreement to proceed with the third reading immediately. I must say I have had no firm answer from the house leaders of the other parties, but I just want to put them on notice that I will make that request.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
maintopic: CHANGE IN ORDER OP BUSINESS FOR TODAY
speechtext:
With regard to the latter part of the statement made by the leader of the house, let me say that if there are no amendments as we go through that particular bill in committee it may be that the house could proceed to give it third reading; it does not appear to be highly controversial.
However, with regard to the other suggested change may I say that this type of alteration at the last moment is unusual and should not be indulged in without adequate reason being produced. We have made our preparations for the discussion of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the resolution dealing with crop insurance and the farm machinery bill. To alter the order throws out the arrangements by which people who are taking these subjects seriously are prepared to act.
I dislike raising objections to alterations such as this, but I have vivid recollections of a slight change being made several years ago and a storm of criticism descending upon me, some of it from members who are still in the house such as the Minister of Trans-
Farm Improvement Loans Act port, and some from a member of the then opposition who is now over in London.
Are these resolutions not being dealt with by the same minister, the Minister of Agriculture? Could they not stay in the order which was announced last night? There is not much purpose in announcing business the night before if a sudden change is to be brought before the house just before the first item of business is called. I lodge my complaint with regard to this manner of organizing the business of the house. It is surely possible to do it in a better way. Alternatively, let us be given an adequate reason why a change should be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: CHANGE IN ORDER OP BUSINESS FOR TODAY
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre in the kindness of his heart does not wish a storm of protest to be raised against me. I am sorry if a few years ago, if the circumstances were almost the same, there was a storm of protest. Perhaps if I had been here I would have convinced my colleagues not to raise it, but I think there must have been a slight difference in the circumstances.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, the reason for my suggesting this slight change is that in our estimation the farm machinery syndicates matter will probably take less time than the crop insurance question; and second, that this is the type of legislation which if brought to a conclusion will be capable of immediate implementation and application. I think that would be sufficient reason for this slight change, together with the fact that I made it clear that today we would take the two measures, so I take it that in their professional conscience all my hon. friends have duly prepared for both matters.
However, Mr. Speaker, if it is felt that any serious inconvenience will be caused, in the circumstances I am sure the Minister of Agriculture would not mind proceeding in the order announced yesterday. But I think for the benefit of the farmers it would be preferable if we could dispose of the farm machinery syndicates resolution right away.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (for the Minister of Finance) moved
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-119, to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this bill is passed I would

Farm Improvement Loans Act like to make a tew remarks with regard to the question of credit generally and how this bill will fit into the credit situation of farmers, and particularly farmers in our area. This bill, of course, doubles the maximum amount that is available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, from $7,500 to $15,000. This legislation is primarily concerned with the doubling of this amount.
All the credit that is now available to agricultural people in Canada is generally divided into two groups; first, short term lending under the Farm Improvement Loans Act; and second, longer term credit under the Farm Credit Corporation. Both these methods of obtaining credit for our farmers leave a gap, in that they are not well coordinated one to the other and farmers sometimes have a great deal of difficulty securing operating capital because their assets are tied up with either the Farm Credit Corporation or under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I say to the minister right away that personally I agree with the increased amount he is making available to farmers through this legislation, but I think his departmental officials, and those in the economics branch of his department particularly, should be considering some method by which there could be more correlation between the kinds of credit that are available to farmers.
The Farm Credit Corporation of course takes a mortgage and it mortgages everything it can get its hands on, regardless of the amount of the loan. I suppose you cannot blame the officials for this, but this is what they do. Therefore, when the farm operator goes to the bank to try to obtain operating capital for his immediate needs, the bank has nothing left that it can take in security or hold, even where it can hold title rather than take chattel mortgages; and of course they cannot do this except under section 88 of the Bank Act.
It is a hardship on farmers when both these things tie up their assets so they cannot obtain additional operating capital which they need on a short term basis. I would also like to point out to the minister that with respect to the Farm Improvement Loans Act we depend upon the activities and policies of the chartered banks to make this money available. We have had several occasions in western Canada when the president of the chartered bank has said "We are not going to give these loans; we are going to tighten up on our funds". The first people to get hurt are the farmers who are trying to borrow money


under the Farm Improvement Loans Act because, of course, the bank makes less money on this type of loan than it does on some other types.
It has happened on occasion that the local bankers in the farming communities have received instructions from their head offices regarding the maximum amount of loan that is set out in the legislation. These managers have been told "You are not to make farm improvement loans over $2,000". I have seen letters to this effect that branch managers have shown me. On occasion farmers have had their programs approved by the bank; then the head office of the bank has sent out a circular to the managers saying "We are not going to lend any more money in farm improvement loans". In this case our farmers have not received the loans for which they have applied.
It is vitally important, if we are to pass this kind of legislation, that we have the cooperation of the banking fraternity in order to make it effective. It is no use at all doubling the amount available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act if the bankers are not going to go along with it. I would hope the minister would make sure that he gets in touch with our banks, because they have made a practice over the years, particularly in western Canada, of cutting off the farmer first of all and worrying about him the least. This of course was the reason for the whole system of farm credit and farm improvement loans being put into operation in the first place; it was because our banks were not looking after the credit needs of the people in agriculture. There is hardly any point in passing legislation to double the maximum amount available if the bankers are not going to make this credit available.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Why wouldn't they?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Because they have done it before in situations of tight money, and they will do it again. The bank managers receive instructions from their head offices to cut down on the farm improvement loans because they are not making any money on them. They have done this under previous Liberal regimes and they did it also when our party was in power. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I have seen letters from the head offices telling the branch managers not to make any farm improvement loans of over $2,000. What is the point of passing legislation providing that the maximum loan available shall be $15,000 if the banks are giving instructions to their man-

agers to curtail the amount of farm improvement loans? To my mind this is the very essence of the legislation. If the banks are going to go along with this program, fine and dandy. If they are not, we are just putting it on paper for nothing.
I would like to know from the minister whether he has had discussions with the chartered banks association and whether they will go along with this program. It is fine and dandy to pass legislation and then go home and tell our farmers, "There is now a maximum amount of $15,000 that is available in loans", but then when the farmer goes into the bank and asks the manager for a loan he finds he will only give him $5,000. There is not much point in passing this legislation unless the banks are prepared to co-operate in this respect.
I would ask the minister again whether he has had any discussions with the chartered banks in this regard. Are they going to make this maximum of $15,000 workable? Are they going to start giving $15,000 in loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act? If they are not, I would point out that not very many farmers in my area have been able to obtain the maximum that is provided already.
The minister may well stand in his place and say that perhaps the farmers do not have sufficient assets to enable them to apply for loans, but it is not a question of assets at all. It is a question of bank policy, and that policy is set by the head offices of the banks which are located primarily in eastern Canada. I suggest the very crux of whether this legislation is going to be worth even passing is whether the banks are going to do the job once we do pass it. We are dependant upon the banks to do so, and in the past they have let us down on more than one occasion when it was vitally important to obtain additional money.
I recall that the last time the banks let the farmers down was during a period when the crops were under snow in western Canada. At that time the bank managers were receiving notices from their head offices directing them to curtail farm loans. Under those circumstances, when the farmer needs money he is not able to get it, in spite of legislation passed by this government.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext: Can you tell us the year of that occurrence?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
That situation occurred in 1962. That was a time when farmers desperately needed credit but the banks were curtailing loans under this legislation, when the maximum loan presumably
Farm Improvement Loans Act available was less than the proposed $15,000. Bank managers followed this course on numerous occasions before the one I mentioned. They adopted this attitude in 1956, and I am sure will do so again unless the minister uses his power and that of the government to stop them from doing so. I think the minister should discuss this situation with the head offices of banks in an attempt to ascertain whether they are going to go along with this proposed increase.
Mr. Speaker, I should like again to refer to the other point I made reference to, regarding the tying up of farmers' assets. When a farmer makes a loan under this legislation his assets are tied up and he is unable to obtain bank credit for immediate needs when he finds it vitally necessary to obtain that credit. The farm improvement loans legislation is primarily aimed at intermediate credit, whereas farm credit legislation is aimed at long term credit. On many occasions a farmer finds it necessary to obtain immediate bank credit for day to day operations.
As one can readily see, there are three different categories of bank credit, treated in three different ways. A farmer may have obtained a loan through the Farm Credit Corporation and at the same time have a mortgage on his land, his machinery and perhaps his cattle. If he goes to the bank to get more bank credit of course he is unsuccessful, because his assets are all tied up.
We can propose legislation, put it on the order paper, debate it, pass it and have it become law, but that does not necessarily mean it will be operative. We must have some assurance from the banks that the purpose envisaged by this proposed increase will be understood and carried out by the banks, and I should like the Minister of Agriculture to make some comment in respect of whether he has had any discussions with the heads of chartered banks in this regard, and whether he can give us some assurance that they are going to help to make this proposed legislation work efficiently.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we are faced with this legislation at the present time I think all hon. members would be remiss if they scrutinized it just in the narrow context of farm loan legislation. I speak particularly at this time for eastern Canadian farmers, and it is my hope that this is not just one isolated piece of legislation but part of the government's larger and broader plan to keep farmers on larger, more economically productive farm units.

Farm Improvement Loans Act
The minister said some days ago in this house that eastern Canadian dairy farmers were better off than they had been for 15 years, and he repeated that on two occasions. Mr. Speaker, that is just not the fact. While it is very interesting for us by this legislation to increase the loan limit to $15,000, many eastern farmers today cannot avail themselves of even the amount presently available. Many farmers in eastern Canada are abandoning their farms, particularly in my area, in spite of the minister's statement that the dairy farmers are well off in eastern Canada. Many of those farmers will be interested in finding out about even a few instances of loans being obtained up to the $15,000 limit under this new legislation.
I suggest this legislation will not be meaningful to many farmers in eastern Canada unless this government commences to make ARDA work. I do not intend to get into an argument on semantics as to whether the Minister of Forestry, with his responsibility for ARDA, is the eastern minister of agriculture. I do not intend to go to any great length in this chamber today to criticize the present government for not getting ARDA working faster and more efficiently in the province of Quebec; because while Ottawa and Quebec wrangle and argue, the plight of the eastern farmer, who so often is abandoning his farm at the present time, does not get any better. I simply say that unless much greater impetus is given to ARDA than has been given by the government in the past, and unless the Minister of Agriculture contacts the Minister of Forestry, who is now in charge of ARDA, and instructs him to get things moving in the province of Quebec at a much faster rate, this legislation before the House of Commons at the present time will not have much meaning to many eastern farmers.
Mr. Speaker, following the statements made by the minister in this house a number of days ago in respect of the improved position of eastern dairy farmers, I visited some farm fairs in my area, and through discussion of the situation with farmers I have ascertained that they are distressed by the fact that someone has apparently informed the minister that they are better off today than they have been for the past 15 years.
This present legislation, coupled with improved ARDA legislation, I hope will enable the Minister of Industry and the Minister of Finance, in co-operation with the Minister of Agriculture, to assist and encourage

farmers to stay on larger farm units which are more economically viable. I hope this present legislation is not an isolated shot in the dark piece of legislation, but that it is well thought out within an integrated plan.
Mr. Speaker, I hope we will see the immediate establishment of vocational training schools in rural areas, because obviously when farms become automated and larger, young people tend to leave them. I hope the government will encourage young people to attend vocational schools in rural areas in order that when they leave the farms they will be trained and able to take their place in industry. I firmly believe it is part of the government's long term plan to keep farmers on larger farm units, and I hope this plan will be worked out in conjunction with a plan to increase vocational guidance and training in rural areas.
I hope the Minister of Industry will also consider, in respect of his area designation program, that tax incentives should be provided in rural areas for the establishment of light and medium manufacturing industries, and that tax incentives should be provided to companies which decide to retrain workers within their own plants and shops.
I am simply saying that while I support this legislation, it will not be effective by itself. I cannot see it will do much good in the long, short or immediate term picture unless it is integrated-call it indicative planning, if you will-with an over-all plan for agriculture in the east. As I said, eastern farmers are not now taking advantage of the present loan limits under this legislation, and because of the generally disastrous situation facing them many have been forced to abandon their farms.
I hope this legislation will be combined with a much greater emphasis on the ARDA legislation than we have seen up to the present time. I hope it is combined with an increase in the building of vocational training schools in rural areas. Again I say that I think the Minister of Industry in his designated area plans can certainly consider the possibility of tax incentives to medium and light industries which decide to establish in depressed rural areas in the east. I also think the Minister of Finance could seriously consider the giving of tax incentives to industries which will retrain workers in light or medium manufacturing industries in rural areas.
While the assumption is that legislation like this will encourage farmers to remain

on more economically productive farm units, we must be realistic and recognize that their sons and grandsons will often be obliged to leave the farms. While this may have to take place, we should make it as attractive as possible in every way for them to remain in rural areas. It is all very well for us at this stage of the scientific revolution to talk about mobility of workers and the necessity for workers and farmers to be willing to move. I understand this. Certainly in an industrial context it is most necessary that many industrial workers and also office workers be willing to be mobile and move in order to advance themselves. The same thing can very often be said of agricultural workers, but at the same time that should not remove from us in Ottawa the responsibility to make it as attractive as possible for our rural people to remain in a rural environment if they so wish.
I hope again that nobody who votes for this legislation will think it is going to work an overnight miracle for eastern farmers, in spite of the fact that the minister says the eastern dairy farmer is better off today than he has been for 15 years.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS INCREASING LOAN MAXIMUM, AGGREGATE OF GUARANTEED LOANS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ever since the present government came into office we have been waiting for the government and particularly the Minister of Agriculture to outline the agricultural program that the government intends to pursue. Various amending bills have been brought in which deal with the periphery of the problem, but we have had no indication that the government is either bringing in or contemplates bringing in any legislation which will grapple with the fundamental problem facing the farmers of Canada.
I think it has to be understood that agriculture today and for the past quarter of a century has been passing through the same kind of technological revolution which confronted industry in the past century. We have seen tremendous changes in agriculture because of the introduction of new agricultural machinery, new methods of farming, the use of electric power on the farms, new varieties of seed and new types of livestock. The result is that the agricultural population has been declining steadily while agricultural production has been going up.
The 1931 census showed that over 30 per cent of the population of Canada lived on farms. In 1961 this had dropped to 11 per cent. This means that a little over 30 years
Farm Improvement Loans Act ago one Canadian out of every three lived on a farm. Today only one Canadian out of every nine lives on a farm. In terms of the labour force there has been a tremendous change and shift in population. Prior to world war II about a million and a quarter persons were in the farm labour force. This has now declined to 650,000, or one tenth of the labour force of Canada. In other words, out of the total labour force only one person in 10 is engaged in agriculture.
The amazing thing is that side by side with this decline in farm population and the farm labour force we have had a tremendous increase in production. Every once in a while we hear some swivel chair farmer saying that the problem of agriculture is that it has to become more efficient. There is no industry in Canada which has increased its productivity at the phenomenal rate which has been achieved by the farmers.
It is estimated that prior to the war one farm worker fed between 10 and 12 persons. Present figures indicate that every person working on a farm feeds about 30 individuals. This is a fantastic increase in productivity. The increase has not been in terms of quantity of goods only, but also in terms of quality of goods, because there has been a great increase in the quality of production. This has been brought about by increasing the size of farms and by the use of expensive machinery which makes it possible for fewer individuals to farm more land and produce more farm produce. No matter what branch of agriculture one investigates one finds that without fail productivity per worker has risen at a very considerable rate.
Alongside this increased productivity a great many problems have been created. Because farms are bigger, and because more expensive equipment is required, the capital investment for land, machinery and equipment per farm unit has increased tremendously. The time has passed when a person with four horses, a cow and a few chickens can start farming. Farming requires a very considerable amount of capital if the farmer is to operate an economic farm unit. Therefore parliament is well advised to give what assistance it can in the field of providing capital.
We have already done this by amendments to the Farm Credit Act. We are now dealing with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, doubling the amount of money which a farmer may borrow from a bank under this legislation from $7,500 to $15,000, as well as increasing the gross amount which may be

Farm Improvement Loans Act borrowed during the present period and increasing the total amount which the government may guarantee under the new period which terminates at the end of June, 1968.
No one can quarrel for a moment with the suggestion the government has made that we should make greater amounts of capital available to farmers for the purchase of land, the purchase of machinery or for the improvement of their buildings and their equipment. I think this is a commendable piece of legislation. However, there is a point I want to make, and I make it with reference to this legislation and equally with reference to the legislation which has to do with the setting up of farm machinery syndicates. Heaven only knows where the minister got the name "syndicates", but we will deal with that when we come to the legislation.
The point I want to make is that legislation making it possible for a farmer to borrow more money to meet his capital needs, legislation to help him make the best use of his machinery, does not even begin to grapple with the central problem that faces the farmer. Almost every speech I have heard the Minister of Agriculture make when introducing legislation or his estimates has stressed the thought that if the farmer got more capital, if he has a larger economic unit, if he improved his livestock or the varieties of seed he uses, this would solve the problem of the Canadian farmer.
No one will deny, Mr. Speaker, that there is value in helping the farmer get increased capital or helping him improve his farming methods or make better use of farm machinery. However, none of these things grapple with the central problem, and the central problem facing the Canadian farmer today is the problem of farm income. Until we come to grips with this problem we are just playing around with the agricultural situation.
One has only to look at two sets of figures to realize how serious the farm income problem is. The dominion bureau of statistics has made all the figures available, and the last figures just came in this morning. If one looks at the index for the prices of agricultural products, one will find that the index commodity figure in 1951 was 296.8. This figure has been declining steadily until in 1961 it reached 261.2. By 1963 it had declined to 259.3. The figures which have just become available today show that as at January 1, 1964 the index figure for agricultural prices was 252.1. From the base year 1951 to 1964 the agriculture price indices have dropped by 44.7 points, and that is a catastrophic drop

in the price which the farmer receives for the products he has to sell.
During the same period there has bsen an alarming increase in the prices which the farmer has been required to pay for the commodities and services which he must buy in order to produce. The dominion bureau of statistics shows that in 1951 the index commodity figure for the goods and services which the farmer purchases stood at 230. By
1962	this figure had risen to 290.8 and by
1963	it had risen to 298.7. As of January 1 of this year the figure was 299.6. This represents an increase from 1951 to 1964 of 66 points in the index commodity figure for the prices of the goods which the farmer must buy in order to stay in business.
If one looks at the income figures, the dominion bureau of statistics prices and price indices, one finds some very interesting facts. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture in its July bulletin prints these figures and makes some comments thereon. They say that:
-the returns of the average Canadian farm operator for his labour and for his capital Investment are only slightly higher, (7.8 per cent) in 1963 than in 1949, while real wages to wage earners have gone up 40 per cent.
They go on to say that:
-the prices of commodities and services used by farmers have gone up consistently since 1949, and in 1963 farm costs showed an increase of about 40 per cent over 1949.
Now, while this report says the average Canadian operator has received 7.8 per cent more in 1963 than he did in 1949, that is in current dollars. If we look at the table put out by the dominion bureau of statistics we find that the realized net farm income in current dollars in 1949 was $1,513,900,000. In 1962 this had declined to $1,490,700,000. The estimate for 1963 is $1,410,200,000.
But if we take the realized farm income in constant dollars and adjust the income each year for price changes, we find that in 1949 the farmers received $1,513,900,000, and by 1959 this had dropped to $977 million. By 1962 this had risen again to $1,074,700,000, and the estimate for 1963 is $986,700,000. In constant dollars, therefore, the realizable net farm income from 1949 to 1963 had dropped from $1,513,900,000 to $986,700,000. If we base this on the average income per operator, during the period from 1949 to 1963 we find that, in 1949 the average income per operator was $2,283, and by 1963 it had risen to $3,519. That is in current dollars, but if we squeeze out the water and make adjustment for price

changes, the income per farm operator only went up from $2,283 in 1949 to $2,462 in 1963.
No industry can possibly stay in business when over a 15 year period, the price of the goods it sells drops by 44 points while the price of the things it has to buy rises by 66 points. No industry whose costs are rising can stay in business when its net realizable income in constant dollars drops in a 15 year period from $1J billion to $986 million. This is the real problem that faces agriculture.
Research, improved strains, better livestock, more modern machinery, larger farm units, ready access to capital, all of these are important but none of them will solve the agricultural problem until the government tackles the question of farm income.
So long as the farmer is caught in a cost price squeeze, so long as he finds the price of everything he has to sell going down while the price of everything he has to buy goes up, and goes up at an alarming rate, then he is doomed to eventual bankruptcy. Lending him money which he has to repay with interest is not going to solve his problem, unless there is some hope that the realizable income he gets will enable him to pay off these loans, and pay his taxes and meet his other costs.
I rose, Mr. Speaker, merely for the purpose of saying that we in the New Democratic party support any measure that will enable farmers to get credit for improving their farms and extending their operations, but we urge the government to bring down some policy to deal with the real farm problem, the problem of farm income, to get the farmer out of the cost price squeeze, to do something about farm costs which are going up, and about farm prices which are going down. Unless the government tackles this problem it is just playing around.
We have had no indication from the Minister of Agriculture that he is even seized of this problem, that he is even conscious there is a problem about farm income, and unless the government does appreciate this problem, tackles it and brings down legislation to provide the farmers with adequate income in relation to their increasing costs, then we are going to continue to have people leaving the farms. We will continue to have farmers going bankrupt, and to have agriculture as one of the depressed industries in this country.
In days gone by we had industrial black areas. Today industry is experiencing a period of boom, but it is a period of industrial boom which surrounds areas of agricultural depression.
Farm Improvement Loans Act
We have cities that are growing and expanding, but our rural areas are going back, and they are going back because the farmers' income will not meet their costs of production and enable them to stay on the farms as efficient producers. Unless the government wakes up to this problem and tackles it, the problem will get worse.
We are not satisfied in this parliament to have the government hand out the soothing syrup, that if only we have more agricultural research and improved livestock strains and better varieties of seed, all our farm problems will disappear. They will not disappear until the government faces up to the problem of the inadequacy of farm income.
Today farmers find that most of the commodities they produce go into the export market where they must be sold in competition, without any protection, without the farmer having any control over the price at which they will be sold. At the same time that the farmer is selling in an unprotected market he is buying in a protected market where almost everything that he purchases has its price set by someone else. That is why he pays more for his machinery and gets less for his products. That is why the farmer is finding it increasingly difficult to meet his outstanding obligations.
We in this party will keep on pressing the government to face up to the problem of agricultural income and, if it does not face up to it, then we will certainly raise our voice repeatedly until the government either admits that it does not know what to do or is not going to do it, or finally resolves to tackle this problem and undertake the only kind of program, that can make agriculture a viable economy, and that is to put the farmers back on their feet and enable them to operate efficiently and to live comfortably on their farms.
The government has to do something about the problem of agricultural income. If it fails to do so the responsibility will lie with it, and the farmers will not be slow to recognize the government's negligence in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, my first words in taking part in this debate are to say that I am not an expert in agriculture, far from it, but coming from an area where agriculture constitutes an important factor in the economy, I think it is my duty to speak in the house on behalf of the thousands of farmers from my

Farm Improvement Loans Act area as well as from the province of Quebec in general.
We have before us a government bill providing for an increase in credit facilities available to farmers. If I look up the order paper, I note that two other measures concerning agriculture are to be considered shortly; both deal also with the need to increase credit available to farmers. In my opinion, this is a serious symptom of what seems to be a lasting disorder. I wonder whether we have the right formula to cure that disorder.
There is a desire to help farmers by all means but the only concrete measures which have been offered till now were all meant to get the farmers more deeply into debt by urging him to invest more in a unit which is already recognized as uneconomic, precisely because it is impossible for the farmer to produce at a cost which would leave him a profit at current market prices.
As the hon. member for Burnaby-Co quit-lam (Mr. Douglas) who just resumed his seat said so well, I think that the farmers whom we now advise to increase their production have proved more than any other sector of our economy that they had anticipated this amazing development of productivity at all levels.
I believe, and there is conclusive evidence to support this statement, that farmers were among the first to improve their production, not only in quantity and in quality, as was stated by the previous speaker, but also in variety, since today, in Canada, they offer a great variety of meat, vegetable, fruit and all other farm products. I think we pay a tribute to the farmers when we recognize the tremendous contribution they made to the economy of this country and also the countless goods they supplied to us through their labour and initiative.
But I think we have not yet found a solution to their problems. I think it is somewhat as desperate people that farmers are now looking up to us. They are wondering whether they really knocked at the right door to get a solution to their problems.
What are we offering them? Easier credit. There is the evidence that they do not have enough income, since we have to offer them sources of cheap money and to guarantee their borrowings.
Is that not proof that their profession today is considered by lenders as not offering enough guarantee, since we feel that the government has to become a surety for them with the banks and other institutions? I

think such a situation is really abnormal. I wonder if you will find now in industry firms with a capital investment of $50,000 to $60,000 which get so little income on an annual basis?
I think that it is in that particular area that we will have to work most; we will have to make the Canadian people understand that they must pay a fair price for the work done by the farmer to produce.
We are ready to pay, in the automobile industry, the manufacturing price plus a certain profit and I cannot understand that the Canadian people do not accept to pay a just and fair price for the farmer's production, although they accept to do it for any manufactured product.
I think that farm production is the very basis of life and that the population must accept to pay a just and fair price for it. At the present time the farmer is in our country the worker who gets the lowest pay for his work.
In my opinion, that is the problem and it is not by providing farmers with credit to enable them to purchase equipment or to enlarge their farms that we will remedy the situation. We are forgetting that the basic problem is one of marketing and of adequate prices for farm products.
It is said that farmers now work for 10 to 15 cents an hour. That is fantastic. A floor sweeper in a plant gets from $2 to $2.25 an hour for unimportant work which, for all practical purposes, requires no special qualification or skills. In comparison with such a salary, the income of the farmer who must support his family is just simply ridiculous. That is why so many farmers leave the farm for the city; they realize that people who have absolutely no qualifications earn much more than they do after a whole year during which their wives and children have worked hard for 10, 12 and 18 hours a day.
We will surely vote in favour of Bill No. C-119 which is before us but that legislation is only a partial solution to the problems of the agricultural industry. When the act was passed in 1945, it certainly met a need and it will definitely be useful for farmers to see the amount of loans available for the purchase of machinery raised from $7,500 to $15,000. However, there is a slight problem that has been brought to my attention by farmers and I should like to speak about it because it concerns the whole field of agriculture.
Nowadays farmers are being asked to diversify their crops. Naturally that calls for the purchase of machinery and farmers are

extended the necessary credit to make the additional investment.
But there is another problem. When they want to buy machinery, they can get a loan from the bank, because the latter gets a lien on the machinery bought and knows moreover that the federal government guarantees reimbursement of the loan. The bank is thus assured that it will not lose anything and the only person who has no such assurance is once again the farmer. The bank has no problem, since it does not run any risk, it does not do any work; on the other hand, the farmer takes all the risks, he is responsible and must work to meet his obligations at the end of the year.
He is the only one under our financial system who is not insured, whose income is not guaranteed. The bank has been assured that it would get 6 per cent interest. There is no doubt that the banks do not want to take any risk; they do not even take the risk of working, they will surely not run the risk of losing money, but the farmer must assume every risk.
When the farmer wants to buy farm equipment, he can do so through this legislation and in order to improve his situation, he is actually asked to diversify his production or to specialize in some field. To this end, farmers must have their production financed on an almost annual basis. In the spring, they must obtain the necessary credit in order to purchase seed grain, lime, fertilizers; they need credit to buy feed grain so as to feed their cattle all through summer and until fall. At present, this type of credit is not available from the banks, which are unwilling to take any chance, because there is actually a risk in that case, since the government does not provide any guarantee. And the banks cannot mortgage the future production, because nobody can guarantee it. Since he is unable to secure a loan on those conditions, the farmer must apply to private institutions, and sometimes even to more or less honest money lenders. In most cases, he has to obtain credit from the large milling enterprises. One knows what it means: farmers must get their feed grain by signing a contract with a mill and commit themselves to buy all their grain there all through summer and until fall. At that time, they unload their crop on the market without knowing its value in advance. There again, mills take no chances, but the farmers run all the risks and have to repay the loans in the fall. If not, they will be dispossessed of everything they own.
Farm Improvement Loans Act
Then, I think that if we really want farmers to profit by this legislation, loans granted by a bank should be guaranteed, because under our present system, the bank cannot lose. But I do not see why we could not take another step forward and guarantee to the banks that they will not lose any money if they grant reasonable loans to farmers to finance their needs throughout the summer until harvest time in autumn.
We should accept that first step, since we have already accepted the principle of guaranteed loans to banks. We should guarantee those loans to banks to enable farmers to elude the control of large millers, enjoy a greater independence and get their feed grain at cheaper prices. In other words, they would be free. They would not be compelled to buy solely from dealers who in most cases are taking unfair advantage of them.
I think that this is the main argument I wanted to develop in my contribution to this debate this afternoon, in short, we should guarantee loans granted by banks to farmers to finance their purchases throughout the year up to harvest time in autumn, in the hope that the farmer would have enough money to his credit to finance his purchases during the year and thus avoid paying 6 per cent interest since, in my opinion, he thus loses any profit realized during the year. Of course, with our present system, this will not come about tomorrow.
So, the solution to this problem would be to ensure for farm products a fair price which would cover production costs plus a reasonable profit as any other production in any other industrial field. Agriculture is a basic industry and therefore it is our responsibility today to see to it that farm products are marketed at a reasonable and fair price.

Mr. Speaker, I could see that the minister was talking with other members, but I was under the impression that he was consulting his colleagues in order to know whether Quebec agriculture still concerned them. That is why I let him go on. I think he will get good advice, because I know those with whom he speaks now and I know they can give him most profitable suggestions for Quebec agriculture. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, those two members are from Ontario and they know Quebec very well, I presume.
I see the Minister of Agriculture has left the house; he will probably consult Quebeckers, which may be more favourable to agriculture in Quebec.
I am not against the increase proposed in Bill No. C-119, but I wonder seriously whether the fact of increasing the loan from $7,500 to $15,000 will really be profitable for Quebec farmers.
One must have lived in our area and accompanied some Quebec farmers to our chartered banks to know the difficulty they experience when they want to borrow $1,000 or $2,000.
Mr. Speaker, is it sincerely believed-as far as I am concerned, I do not believe it at all, take my word for it-that in the coming months or years, farmers will dare borrow up to $15,000 from chartered banks? This is impossible in 98 per cent of the cases in the province of Quebec, especially when one knows all the investigations conducted by the banks in connection with such loans and all the guarantees they require. In fact some banks require as collateral more than three or four times the amount of money they are risking by granting some loans to farmers.
I know beforehand that in 98 per cent of the cases, this bill will not be to the advantage of our farmers in the province of Quebec, not because the legislation is not good, but rather because the chartered banks are the only judges, in brief, the ultimate judges in all these loans, just like they are for all the transactions they enter into with the farmers.
It is all very well to say in this house that we grant loans to farmers, and we do this and that in order to allow our farmers to get into debt. But what are we actually doing? We are simply acting as sales agents between the chartered banks and our farmers. That is all we are doing in this house. We incite the

farmers to get into debt with the chartered banks. Moreover, the government guarantees such loans, not in order that the farmers may not lose anything, but above all in order that the chartered banks may not lose anything.
The federal government guarantees the loans, and we are asking our farmers to get into debt so that two, three, four or at the most ten years from now, their properties will not belong to them any more and they will be so indebted that they will have to sell everything and seek refuge in the city.
Furthermore, I have had occasion to witness this in numerous cases, as far as loans from the Farm Credit Corporation are concerned. As a matter of fact, some farm loan counsellors, seemingly competent, told a farmer who owned four lots and more than 250 acres of land under cultivation: "You had better sell your farm and go to the city". I have heard that dreadful remark with my own ears and I would like to draw it to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture who, once again, unfortunately, is not in the house. However, I hope he will read my remarks, for I have already pointed out to the house the doings of certain farm loan counsellors whom I had qualified as not being serious, as amateurs, as people who sometimes are touring the country with their wives telling this or that farmer who has no gravel yard or no sidewalk in front of his house: "You are too poor to obtain a loan, go to the city".
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that as long as we have that kind of men and, as I said in one of my articles, men from the cities trying to show the farmers how to live on a farm, we shall always be faced with failures such as the one we are encountering at present. And this will last until the government awaken and realize that they must send competent technical advisers to the farmers so as to see that these loans will enable them to live, for some years at least, on their farms.
Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that we were merely selling agents. I am asking the government to try, at least in that capacity, to have their say with the banks as far as these loans are concerned.
It has often been claimed that the government controls the banks. This is 8 per cent true. Now, the government might at least control them in so far as directing them to give the farmers a fairer deal.
Moreover, if the government undertakes to guarantee farm improvement loans it should see to it that the farmer who needs only $4,000, $5,000 or $6,000 to raise 20220-509
Farm Improvement Loans Act the yield of his farm by 50 per cent, obtains those sums. At present, the bank manager will offer him only $2,000, whereas he needs $5,000 or $6,000. That is a way of refusing a loan, because the farmer is bright enough to know that a $2,000 loan will often put him in a worse position than before.
For instance, a farmer wants to develop a business of his own-I say of his own, because I am not speaking of such business firms as exist at this time in my country, such as commercial hatcheries, piggeries, flour mills, or any other large animal producing business making a good profit. Indeed, at the end of the year, when the farmers have worked hard, night and day, for those companies, they find that they have earned a salary of about $1800 to $1900 to maintain a family of 10 or 12 children. And we think that this is fine. And we leave the entire control to those large companies or mills which establish profit-making farm production here and there. And then, we are told in this parliament: All is well, farm production is increasing. We are told that it is increasing, but it is always to the advantage of the centralizer, the capitalist, and not of the small farmer.
Mr. Speaker, we in Quebec are able to produce. But I say, even if it should surprise some people, that the crucial point, in Quebec farming today, is not necessarily to accelerate production. To my mind, the capital question is marketing.
I was brought up on a farm, and I know that the farmer's problem in the fall consists in disposing of his products at a reasonable price.
If today we may congratulate ourselves that there is prosperity in the west, it is mainly for this reason: Not only is western production very large, but its marketing is excellent. The west succeeded in establishing the Canadian wheat board, with the help of the governments. Should the Canadian wheat board be abolished in that part of Canada, I am sure that the living standard of our western farmers would decline by 50 per cent.
What do we really need in Quebec? A sound marketing policy so that farmers can be sure that they will sell their products at an economic price.
I am sure that when we have succeeded in giving Quebec a sound marketing policy with economic prices, Quebec farmers will not be reluctant to produce, production will come automatically and in large quantity, as is the case in the west.

Farm Improvement Loans Act
Look at the variety of farm produce in the province of Quebec. In a few years, thanks to this marketing policy and government help, the producer will be more prosperous. It is what has taken place in the west. When the Canadian wheat board was set up, farmers made an effort and that effort was supported.
In my area, I know several groups which work hard, but their efforts are supported neither by the provincial government nor by the federal government. And I must say that in this field the work of the provincial government in co-operation with the federal government is badly directed.
I will give only one example: the blueberry farm program under ARDA. One after the other, the federal and provincial ministers visit the area and say: We have invested more than $3 million in blueberry farms; look how wonderful it is.
Precisely, Mr. Speaker, this is the mistake that is made. Production and overproduction are looked after, and no attention is given first to marketing.
We have set up more than 14 or 15 of these blueberry areas. But, try to find out anything about them. Nobody dares mention them, because nothing has been produced. There has not been anything other than the personal efforts of those who worked for the marketing.
If, this year, blueberries sold a little better, it is due to the fact that two or three private organizations took the matter in hand-and I want to say it in this house-without any kind of help from any government, while we spent $3 million-I am not the one to say it, Mr. Speaker, it is the ministers-in an attempt to set up blueberry patches. However, there was not a cent spent for marketing, not one cent.
I just heard a remark. Since farming now comes under forestry, I say to the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) that it would have been better for him to appropriate $1.5 million for marketing and $1.5 million for the development of blueberry fields, in order to help those already operating blueberry fields, instead of systematically destroying the forests.
Tremendous projects have been set up lately. Trees are cut down over hundreds of acres of forest lands in order to grow blueberries. Exactly the opposite should be done. Those who were entrusted with this problem know nothing about blueberries and therefore, they were unsuccessful this year, because out of 14 blueberry fields, not one yielded a profitable crop.

which the farmers need to operate their farms.

That fund will be made available, even for marketing, through the facilities of the Bank of Canada. Let us stop lending through private banks, that is chartered banks; let us stop always depending on them to try and get our economy moving. In advance, we are sure that chartered banks will start moving their own economy before the economy of the country.
We have a bank in this country, an institution that belongs to us. Why not use it to help agriculture, which is the basic industry in our country? Now that the Minister of Agriculture is back in his seat, I am sure that he will take the remarks I just made into serious consideration, in order to arrive at some understanding of the needs of agriculture in Quebec and then act as quickly as possible, so as to rectify the farmers' situation in that province, because if we want to put a stop to the rural exodus towards the cities, the federal Department of Agriculture, together with the provincial minister of agriculture, must absolutely try to find a much more serious solution than all those proposed to this date.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a few remarks on this Bill No. C-119 and I intend to restrict my remarks to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I come from a province in which these farm improvement loans are greatly appreciated. One of the reasons for this appreciation is that these loans are made by the banks in times of emergency. In my province crops are very uncertain things. In 1960 or 1961 when we had snowed under crops, many farmers availed themselves of these loans. The same situation could occur this year. At one time we thought we had a very good crop and farmers had no intention of borrowing money. Now, after these heavy frosts, our farmers may have to again avail themselves of these loans. They may have to use the frozen grain as feed for livestock or by going into hog production. In this way they will realize a better return from the grain than by selling it to the Canadian wheat board.
I am pleased to note that the size of the loan has been increased from $7,500 to $15,000. In the past we have found that a loan of $7,500 was not sufficient to enable farmers to invest in new machinery such as grain dryers, which may be needed this year. I was home over the long week end, and it had been raining for three or four days. The prospects were that it might rain for another three days. This means that the crop, which is ready to be combined, is going to be damp and tough. Farmers may be able to make use of these loans by buying grain dryers. As I have said, this is very important because you can go to your bank or credit union and avail yourself of these loans. I regret that this legislation was not introduced a year ago to increase the amount of the loan to $15,000. Western agriculture today is highly mechanized and a loan of:

Farm Improvement Loans Act $7,500 is not large enough to enable farmers to buy certain implements, such as combines.
As I have said, the farmers make use of these loans in cases of emergency. I appreciate too the fact that the loan fund has been increased from $400 million to $500 million. Another thing I should like to stress is that when livestock is purchased these loans are available for a period of ten years. When conditions are such that there may be a drop in farm income, the banks are often reluctant to extend this credit to farmers. Mr. Speaker, like many of the other members in the house I want to congratulate the government for introducing this legislation at this time. This amendment will result in an increase in the amount available under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and this is something to which the farmers have been looking forward for the last 16 or perhaps 20 months. A great change has taken place during that period in the type of machinery that the farmers are likely to use.
There were some of us who thought this legislation might have been dealt with earlier in this present session. This draws to our attention the importance of the priority that is given legislation in the House of Commons. I felt the government would have been well advised to have brought this legislation forward before introducing the farm credit legislation and then this legislation would have been of some use to the farmers during this harvest period. This was one of the pieces of legislation that was on the statute books when the government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) took office.
After that the government led by him retained this as a part of the over-all agricultural policy of the country, and made certain improvements to it. In its initial stages it provided loans of something like $3,000 and now, under the terms of this bill, loans up to $15,000 will be provided. This indicates something of the inflation that has taken place in the price of farm land, and also something of the increased capital costs for anyone engaging in agriculture.
I would like to commend the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Brown) on his reference that this legislation alone is not enough. I should also like to commend the hon. mem-

ber for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) and the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard), who drew attention to the government's failure to tackle the problems facing Quebec farmers. Each of these members has indicated to the government that what farm people need more than anything-and I am not at all decrying the value of this measure-is attention to the problem of marketing their products.
We in this party are proud of the record achieved by our government when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), who is presently in his seat, was minister of agriculture. One of the members of the Ralliement Creditistes mentioned the problem producers had in getting a market for blueberries, and this is only one of the marketing problems.
I was interested in the remarks of the leader of the New Democratic party (Mr. Douglas) as we in this party have also been waiting for the minister to indicate the agricultural philosophy and general policies of the government. Having these minor amendments brought in on a piecemeal basis is hardly fair to members of the house when they are considering the over-all effect of an agricultural program. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few words to say following the remarks made by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) and the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis), as far as the number of loans made in the province of Quebec is concerned.
Farm Improvement Loans Act
I have no intention whatsoever to defend the government or to attack the hon. member for Villeneuve, but I feel it is necessary to set the record straight concerning certain figures in the 1962 and 1963 reports.
First of all, in 1961, 11,126 loans amounting to $18,101,149 were granted in the province of Quebec; in 1962, 3,244 loans amounting to $5,515,926 were granted; in 1963, 2,871 loans amounting to $5,958,713 were granted. If there was a decrease it is due to the fact that in 1960 the government of the province of Quebec passed a legislative measure-before the Union Nationale lost power-allowing the provincial government to pay up to 3 per cent of the interest on the loans granted by banks and caisses populaires for the purchase of machinery or for the improvement of farms in the province.
That legislation enabled the farmer to borrow up to $4,000 for the purchase of machinery, farm improvement, the construction of buildings, etc., and up to $3,000 for the purchase of livestock. This means that the Quebec farmer availed himself to the maxi-num of the farm improvement legislation till 1961. Then he somewhat broke away from it to borrow from banks and caisses populaires through the provincial act, because with the latter he could avail himself of a subsidy of 3 per cent granted by the provincial government, so that he had only 3 per cent interest to pay on loans secured under the provincial act.

They took full advantage of it until 1960 to improve their farms and their operations. Farm Improvement Loans Act the 3 per cent grant from the provincial government.
I repeat it, Mr. Speaker, no one must get the impression that there was any discrimination against the Quebec farmers. The only reason why the number of loans decreased is the one I just gave.
But with the amendment which the federal government is presenting today, increasing the maximum from $7,500 to $15,000, the number of loans will probably increase, because the maximum now allowed by the Quebec legislation is $7,000, that is $4,000 for the improvement or purchase of farm implements and $3,000 for the purchase of livestock, which is not enough for a farmer with a large operation.
Just the same, I wish to point out that I think this legislation should have been presented to us several months ago, because if I am not mistaken-I speak from memory- that resolution has been on the order paper since July 11. Several farmers became interested in it and asked members on the government side as well as members in the opposition to put pressure on the Minister of Agriculture so that this bill could be discussed as soon as possible. I think, Mr. Speaker, that within a few days, this legislation will be passed, but before it has gone through all stages, it surely will be too late, in certain areas, to take full advantage of it. Indeed, by the end of September or by October, farmers will not be as interested as they were in July or August to purchase some machinery they need, or to carry out some improvement on their farm. It is on that point that I wish to criticize the government for not having introduced this legislation sooner. We are going to accept it readily, but it is most unfortunate that they had to wait until now to bring it before the house.
Also I take this opportunity to tell the government that since they took office the only legislation they brought forward in the field of agriculture were amendments to existing legislation. I appreciate that amendments had to be made to those measures, but that is not what the farmer wants nowadays. He is asking for completely new legislation that will improve the lot of farmers in eastern Canada and more particularly, as far as I am concerned, the lot of farmers in the province of Quebec.
To conclude, I wish to say this: all these amendments, even if they are satisfactory, could not be compared to legislation which could be passed to assist the eastern farmers. I refer to legislation concerning the dairy


industry, because it is the basic industry of farming in eastern Canada just as wheat growing is the basic income of western farmers.
We are able to pass practical legislation for the farmers. I should like the government to refer to the remarks made in this house by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) and by myself on July 10 last, because if the government really wants to help the eastern farmer, who is now in need of help, it will have to consider the field of dairy farming in order to introduce new legislation. I am sure that this would solve the existing problem and thus, really help the eastern farmers.
