speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member for an important agricultural area of western Canada it gives me great pleasure this afternoon to make a few comments during this debate about this proposed amendment to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I was disappointed that this piece of legislation was not introduced prior to the legislation dealing with the Farm Credit Corporation because, as was mentioned I believe by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasser-den), a lot of beneficial effects have been lost for this particular year. However I am very pleased to see at last that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) has introduced another piece of legislation which will help to bolster the agricultural economy.
Mr. Speaker, this piecemeal policy in respect of agricultural legislation, to which we have been exposed by this government, is a far cry from the policy laid down by the right hon. leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), when he was prime minister, and in the statement he made I believe in August, 1958, when he laid down a comprehensive national agricultural policy including various measures such as the crop insurance Agricultural Stabilization Act, farm credit, water conservation, amendments to the Seeds Act, human slaughter of animals, and other measures dealing with a multitude of problems facing the agricultural industry. Today we find we are dealing with only the second piece of legislation introduced by this government in respect of the agricultural economy.
Mr. Speaker, today I think my remarks could be related to a statement made by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in a presentation made to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) under date of February 26, 1964. As you will realize, the Canadian

Federation of Agriculture represents and speaks for something in the neighbourhood of 500,000 Canadian farmers. That federation presented its brief last February and I should like to read several excerpts dealing with the subject of farm credits. Stated in this brief is the following:
The federation, at the federal-provincial agricultural conference in December of last year, made a number of submissions on farm credit to the government, urging in general much more intensive attention to farm credit needs, and the development of new programs.
I will not repeat these representations here in full, Mr. Speaker, but in the resolutions delegates to the annual meeting laid special emphasis on three immediate needs which I should like to draw to the attention of the house at this time. Those needs are stated in this brief as follows:
First, they reiterated our long standing request for special disaster loan legislation.
This matter is now under study by the Farm Credit Corporation, and the federation is looking forward to early action in this regard.
The brief then goes on to state:
No interest should be charged for the first year at least, and very low interest for an appropriate period, perhaps five years.
Second, the loan limit of the Farm Credit Corporation should be raised to $50,000.
Of course, the house has dealt with that matter and as we are aware, this has been increased to a maximum of $55,000.
The third suggestion in this brief dealing with farm credit relates to the discussion we are having this afternoon, and states:
Third, the loan limit on farm machinery under the Farm Improvement Loans Act should be raised to $10,000-
Mr. Speaker, this point was dealt with a few moments ago by my illustrious colleague, the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent), and I think his point was very well taken.
This section of the federation's brief in respect of farm credit concludes as follows:
May we repeat that we feel well-developed, flexible credit services to meet farm needs are of utmost importance and deserve more intensive investigation and research than they have received in the past.
Earlier this afternoon the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Homer) made a very valid point when dealing with policy, as far as the application of these loans is concerned. I should like to refer to the annual report of the Farm Improvement Loans Act for 1963. Perhaps I should tell the minister that I 20220-510
Farm Improvement Loans Act am pleased this report was forthcoming. Yesterday when I was looking up some information in respect of this subject I had to refer to the 1962 report, and wondered at the time why there was a laxity in that the 1963 report was not available. We are happy to have received it this afternoon, even though the debate has been under way for some time.
Under the heading "Review of lending operations since inception" this annual report states:
The average size of loans has increased from $784 in 1945 to $1,757 in 1963.
It is interesting to note at the outset that $784 is a very low average, although perhaps it is compatible with the year 1945, and the fact that this was new legislation at that time. However, 19 years later we find that the average size of loans has only increased to $1,757. The comparable figure for 1962 is $1,626. In other words during that year the average loan has only increased approximately $125.
I should now like to refer to the point emphasized by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. Apparently the lending institutions are taking too tough an attitude in their consideration of applications that come to them, because in looking at the 1963 report in respect of loans made under this legislation we find that they continue to be low. The report goes on to state:
The total amount of all claims paid to the banks under the guarantee represents about one tenth of 1 per cent of the total amount of loans made to date.
I believe that is a remarkable record and indicates that the government has not incurred any great loss in respect of loans made under this legislation. The government has incurred only a minimum loss. A total of $207,622 has been recovered on claims paid as of 1963, including $39,421 which was collected in 1963.
I think the banks should be more flexible and tolerant in their consideration of these applications. I notice this statement at the end of the report in reference to bank loans:
The banks continue to extend their co-operation in the implementation of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Rural branch banks have established many outstanding lending records in various agricultural areas across Canada. Several individual branch banks, for instance, have made farm improvement loans under this act in excess of $4,500,000. Operations under this legislation have, however, not been confined to rural banks. Farm improvement loans are made by a number of branch banks in smaller cities.
I should like to emphasize the last expression by repeating it: "-a number of branch

Farm Improvement Loans Act banks in smaller cities". I presume they mean that a number of these banks have established good lending records. I do not think that in itself is good enough. The banks of this country have an enviable record, of which we are proud, and they play a very important part in the successful economy of the agricultural industry as a whole. These leading institutions have a definite responsibility under this act to see that there is no discrepancy or variation in policy between one bank and another, and between one area and another. There should be laid down a general policy so that all banks many establish good records in this lending field, rather than just a few. I should like to emphasize the fact, referred to so aptly by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson, that there has been something wrong in the operation of this legislation, in view of the fact that we are today considering an amendment to increase maximum loans to $15,000. Yet, as I say, in looking at the figures we find that the average loan is only $1,757, so the act is not doing the job that we as legislators intended it to do. I think that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) have to take this matter under serious consideration and encourage the lending institutions to take a much more tolerant attitude toward the needs of the agricultural industry.
I was going to go into a more extensive review of the lending operations but this has been done very adequately by previous speakers. In my opinion the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) gave a very forthright review of the need for credit in the province of Quebec, and other speakers this afternoon also dealt with credit needs. Personally I am very much in favour, and I think the agricultural industry in general is too, of the legislation that has been introduced into the house today to make more money available through increasing the limit on loans and also increasing the amount of money available for lending. The necessity was impressed on me as a member of the standing committee on agriculture both two and three years ago when we were inquiring into the cost of farm machinery and were considering how farm credit affected the agricultural industry as a whole.
In the evidence presented to the committee something came out that I thought was very pertinent and important to the committee and the agricultural industry in general. Evidence was given that a great number of farmers who were purchasing machinery on credit


were getting credit through subsidiary loan companies established by the farm machinery companies. In other words, in order to promote the sale of farm machinery on a credit basis the machinery companies were providing credit facilities and credit was not being secured by these farmers under the Farm Credit Act or the Farm Improvement Loans Act. When we inquired into the reason for this situation we were alarmed to find that in many cases farmers were paying from 11 to 13 per cent for the use of money in order to buy farm machinery to equip their farms properly.
To my mind this was a very significant fact and I believe I made the comment at that time that we should look immediately at the farm credit situation so far as farm improvement loans were concerned, and increase the amount of money available for the purchase of farm machinery which money, as hon. members know, is made available at an interest rate of 5 per cent. The interest rate of 5 per cent is in effect over the four year period, which is the period for which the farmer borrows money under the Farm Improvement Loans Act in order to purchase machinery. The difference between an interest rate of 5 per cent and a rate of 11 to 13 per cent that many farmers were paying to the subsidiaries of machinery companies would mean a vast saving.
I wish to emphasize again that the banks must take a more flexible and tolerant view of applications. I also emphasize that we are pleased that this legislation has been brought before the house. I trust it will be passed as soon as possible so that the money will be available to our farmers who need it so badly.

However the house will appreciate that the bill deals only with one aspect, namely farm credit.
The hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) wanted to know whether the banks are co-operating with farmers who apply for loans. This question was also raised by the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. Southam). The only answer I can give, of

course, is to be found in the report itself, which shows that the number of loans has increased steadily over the years, that the size of loans has increased and that the aggregate principal amount of money for guaranteed loans in the present lending period will have to be increased from $400 million to $500 million. I respectfully suggest that this is powerful evidence that there has been a good measure of co-operation between bank managers and farmers, although I am the first to admit that there may be isolated cases in which this co-operation has not been forthcoming.
I am indebted to the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska (Mr. Vincent) for the very lucid answer he gave to the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) regarding the discrepancy between the amount of loans being made in the province of Quebec and the amount in other provinces. I just wish to say to hon. members from Quebec that, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska, there is no discrimination against the farmers of that province.
One of my colleagues made reference to the fact that some of the merits of the act have been detracted from by the fact that there have been improper farm valuations. With great respect I say to my colleague that I do not think this criticism applies to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, although it may be a valid criticism so far as the Farm Credit Act is concerned. As I did not detect any note of hostility toward the bill now before us I think I should conclude my remarks and respectfully anticipate speedy passage in the committee stage.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, considered in committee and reported.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
20220-510J
Farm Machinery
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the extension of credit to farm machinery syndicates for the purchase of farm machinery and for the terms and conditions of such loans, the amount of a loan not to exceed 80 per cent of the actual price to the farm machinery syndicate of the farm machinery to be purchased with the loan; and to provide also for the establishment in the consolidated revenue fund of a special account not to exceed $25,000,000 to which shall be charged advances made to the Farm Credit Corporation and to which shall be credited all moneys paid to the Receiver General by the corporation and for other financial provisions in relation to the said fund in connection with the administration of the measure.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION OF CREDIT FOR PURCHASES BY SYNDICATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution before us for consideration today proposes a type of farm credit which is fundamentally different from all previous credit programs in Canada. We are all aware of the rapid developments that have taken place in agriculture in the past 20 years, and in particular the developments with regard to the types of farm machinery and equipment available for use on our farms today. We know the value of this machinery to the farmers, both in its ability to save manual labour and in its ability to provide the farmer with the timeliness of operation which is so essential to successful agricultural production. Unfortunately we are all also aware of the high cost of a full line of equipment on a farm today.
When a farmer purchases a modern farm implement he very frequently finds that if he purchases an efficient machine it is able to handle considerably more work than he has for it. He may pay the cost, and sometimes a rather high cost, of a machine which he may use only a limited period during the year, and the capital represented by the machine, which could be used to good advantage for other purposes, must remain idle for long periods. It thus becomes a very expensive machine for him to own unless he expands his farm operations greatly. Probably more than any other single factor, the increased cost of modern farm machinery has made it difficult for the small farmer to make his way and earn a reasonable living under today's conditions.
One of the ways in which farmers can reduce their machinery costs is by sharing equipment with their neighbours, either by sharing in the ownership and use of equipment or by obtaining it on a custom or rental basis for the period of time required. Cooperative use of farm machinery is not new.

Farm Machinery
Many farmers presently share the ownership of individual machines or have work done on a custom basis. It is highly desirable, however, that facilities be provided to enable farmers to organize groups for this purpose on a formal basis and to provide the credit facilities necessary for such groups to procure machinery for the joint use of their members.
The proposed measure will provide for the establishment of a revolving fund of $25 million to be administered by the Farm Credit Corporation. The farm machinery syndicates set up under the provisions of this measure will be able to borrow up to 80 per cent of the cost of the machinery they wish to buy. In this way three or more farmers, each of whom might find it difficult to buy all the machinery they require to operate their farms individually, may join together in a syndicate to buy items of machinery of sufficient capacity to do the work of all members. Furthermore, the farm machinery syndicates will be able to make the machinery which they have purchased available for use by other farmers on a rental or custom basis. In this way farmers who are not members of farm machinery syndicates may still obtain benefit from the proposed measure because of the availability of machinery from such syndicate for use on their farms.
Adequate credit facilities are an important need of Canadian agriculture. We now have the Farm Credit Act to provide long term mortgage credit for the establishment of economic farm units. We have the Farm Improvement Loans Act to provide operating credit for individual farmers. Both of these have been, or are in the course of being, amended at this session to increase their usefulness to farmers. As I stated during the debate on the bill to amend the Farm Credit Act, we have set up an interdepartmental committee to keep the credit needs of farmers under continuing review. The present measure will in my opinion provide an additional and valuable supplement to the present farm credit facilities, and will make a substantial contribution to the welfare of Canadian agriculture.
This is the thought behind the bill which introduces the farm machinery credit act. If we can adopt the resolution, Mr. Chairman, then we could present the bill which certainly covers the proposal in a great deal more detail.

myself by saying that one of the tremendous unsolved problems of the agriculture industry has been rising costs in general and those of machinery in particular. I was planning to put on the record some of the figures that bear out this statement, and then go on to discuss the principle of this particular measure to see how far it moves into the field of meeting this problem. I should like to keep my remarks coherent, so I shall deal with that part of them after the dinner recess.
I should like to point out to the committee that on several occasions in the last 30 years governments have sought to find some answer to the rising costs of machinery. I think all of us recognize that the agriculture revolution during the last 30 or 40 years has been sparked by the mechanization of our farms. I think it is fair to say, generally speaking, that this mechanization hit the prairies first, because they seem to lend themselves to the rapid change-over to mechanization. I think it is recognized also that the move toward mechanization in the twenties was checked by the depression and the war. Since about 1945, western Canada has demonstrated the tremendous willingness of the farm people to risk their future livelihood by borrowing money and by translating this money into modern farm machinery, not only to increase their productivity but to lower the per unit cost of production. The same trend has now become apparent in the central provinces, and I think it will soon spread to all parts of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I
adjourned the debate at six o'clock I was outlining briefly the characteristic that has been most outstanding in agriculture during the last 40 years, namely the use of machinery in the agricultural revolution that has taken place in our country as well as in others. This machinery that I have been talking about as the main ingredient of the agricultural revolution has been very costly, and to date the farmers of Canada have poured over $10 billion into farm investment to try and make their industry more efficient.
To deal more precisely with the resolution under discussion tonight, I went back in my

reading to the several sources that are available to members of the house. One is the fact, as I said earlier, that the costs of farm machinery have exercised people in government circles for many years. I personally recall at least four farm machinery investigations into the cost of equipment, and one of them was being conducted during the period of the government preceding this one, in the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. For two years practical farmers on that committee tried to get the figures of their costs from farm machinery companies, tried to get from distribution agencies estimates of what it cost to handle this machinery with present techniques, and tried to find practical ways of reducing the cost of machinery to farmers.
Since the change of government the standing committee on agriculture and colonization has been called together, but not once has the matter of farm machinery been referred to that committee, and I gather from what the Minister of Agriculture said this afternoon that very little reading of the records of that committee was done before this resolution was introduced. Later in my remarks I shall make this point even more emphatically.
Another source of information is the royal commission appointed in Saskatchewan, called the royal commission on agriculture and rural life. I remember very distinctly in the years after the war, with the sudden rush of mechanization in western Canada and the rising price of farm machinery, that this was one of the greatest single issues facing leaders of various parties and governments in power, and the government of Saskatchewan, realizing the tremendous need for examination into the whole revolution in agriculture, set up this royal commission which sat for four years, from 1952 to 1956.
I know many hon. members have spent a great deal of time looking over the 14 volumes of that royal commission's report. Volume 2 deals with mechanization and farm costs, and even though this volume deals in generalities I think the conclusions arrived at in the royal commission's report are not only true in many parts of Canada which are just going through the revolution of the mechanical age on farms, but will also be true for many of the areas that have still to go through that revolution.
One thing that intrigued me this afternoon as I listened to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam put the finger on the federal
Farm Machinery
government, urging it to tackle the problem of farm income or else his party would continually press for that action, was that these were exactly the same words as I heard him use 20 years ago. Because looking at this problem as an outsider for many years, the thing that struck me about the attitude of the C.C.F. party, now the N.D.P., is that it pointed the finger at the federal government and always held it responsible for farm income.
Generally speaking I believe that this is correct, that rightly or wrongly, the federal government has assumed responsibility over the years for farm income; but it so happens that on this question of action on farm machinery costs, which is recommended in various circles, it is usually only in the constitutional field controlled by the provinces that the definitive and final action can be taken.
It is rather interesting to look at this royal commission report of eight years ago and ask ourselves how much was done in Saskatchewan about its recommendations. I shall not go through the whole 31 conclusions; I will just deal with the recommendations at the end of the report, where the first recommendation urged reform within the farm equipment industry and distribution system as it now exists. The distribution, as it now exists at the consumer level, can only be controlled under property and civil rights by a province.
A second recommendation was that cooperative manufacturing and distribution be examined as a way out of the dilemma, and a third recommendation was nationalization of the industry. This would probably be in the field of federal power, if you are going to do it on a federal basis, but actually constitutionally the power lies only with the provinces.
Looking back over the last eight years we see there was certainly no atempt in Saskatchewan, which is the leading province so far as mechanization is concerned, to nationalize the industry. Of course it was impossible for the Saskatchewan government to do this, because if it nationalized industry in Saskatchewan it would have been called socialist. No socialist government would ever dare to be called socialist, so it shied away from that alternative.
The commission recommended co-operative manufacturing and distribution. There is, Mr. Chairman, one company in existence, C.C.I.L.-Canadian Co-operative Implements

Farm Machinery
Limited-which is set up on the basis of co-operative distribution of the products of one of the manufacturers. It is spread pretty widely through the west and has made a tremendous effort to gain the advantages of co-operative distribution in a very wide area of the country; but if you are objective in your observation of this operation you have to agree it has not been successful, and there are various reasons for that. As to the first recommendation, I think something was done on those lines in Saskatchewan under an act dealing with the distribution of farm machinery in that province. Regulations were changed and tightened up, in consequence of which I believe some 200 merchants engaged in the distributive side of the industry were squeezed out of operation; the regulations prescribed in detail what they had to do if they were to retain their licences to distribute machinery. Apart from that, very little was done in Saskatchewan. I mention this because in my opinion a solution to this problem of machinery costs will not be resolved by one government or another; there needs to be a co-operative approach by governments in both realms of jurisdiction.
I make these comments as an introduction to the general discussion of this resolution. I believe there are in this house a large number of members who have had long experience in farming. Many of them have mechanized their operations completely. Many of them know the problems of financing and the difficulty of equipping farms with modern machinery while keeping costs low enough to enable them to stay in the competitive business of agriculture today. The experience of these members represents a wealth of human resources which could be applied to this task, and from the evidence of the work of the committee on agriculture and colonization over the last few years it appears that the committee had begun to think of a full series of practical suggestions to improve the distribution of farm machinery and reduce costs. I should like to suggest at this point that the bill before us should go before the committee on agriculture so that we may have the benefit of the tremendous amount of knowledge available on the subject in this house. Admittedly, most of the members who have this experience are on the opposition side, but there are several government supporters with practical experience in mixed farming and I am sure they could use this knowledge to assist the efforts of the minister to solve this problem.
I heard only part of the minister's introductory remarks. I gather they were in line

with the resolution before us. We are all wondering what the word "syndicate" means. Some of us thought immediately of Spain in the days of the anarchists when syndicalism was prominent among the social and political ideas of the day. But obviously, on reflection, this is not what the minister has in mind. The expression means some grouping of farmers. I do not suppose there is anything in farming which is harder than persuading farmers to work together. In my personal experience even men who have fought side by side during the war as comrades on the field of battle, and who returned to farming after the war was over, found such co-operation impossible to achieve. With that sort of background one would think they could work together and utilize the same machinery. Yet those same men who served as friends during the greatest of difficulties fell into hostility and enmity when they had to make joint use of farm machinery. In the early days, the trouble arose largely over the use of separators. Farmers would get together and buy a separator. Then, under the pressure of fall weather, the fights which occurred, in many cases between friends of long standing, made them enemies for life. This same difficulty has marked shared farming operations in all parts of Canada. The only time such programs seem to work is when those engaged in them are connected by a blood relationship or when the partners are unusually congenial. After all, it is hard for a man, when his whole year's wages depend on a successful harvest operation, to wait his turn under a pooling arrangement.
This is a difficulty which we must expect. To refer to the situation in Saskatchewan once again, a serious and sincere effort was made after the war on the part of many people to set up a co-operative type of farming. The failures, which were legion, almost always came down to this question of people getting along together. Success was encountered only when those concerned were of a congenial nature, accepting the leadership of whomever they had appointed or elected. No government should be condemned on account of this human frailty. It is a fact which has to be faced when we are considering what is likely to happen in connection with this legislation.
I, for one, intend to support this measure. I do so because I do not think there is any problem which is more vexatious on the cost side of agriculture today than is the cost of machinery. So I think the effort we find here should be supported. I have warned the

house about the difficulty likely to be encountered when a group of farmers is brought together. I hope farmers will accept the logic of the situation-that the use of one set of machinery for a certain operation spread over five farms is more economic than the possession by each of the five farmers of his own equipment. I will submit a corollary to the point I have made about the difficulty of getting people to co-operate. It seems we must accept the fact that certain farming operations must necessarily be carried on when the weather is right. Then we should accept the principle that in relation to these operations a farmer must have his own machinery, his individual possession. If we accept this, then I believe we would make a step toward wisdom by letting him have it, even though logic says farmers would be better off if they pooled their operation. The operation I have in mind is, primarily, harvesting, though my remarks apply also to certain types of seeding and cultivation equipment. However, there a number of operations, particularly in mixed farming on modern farms which lend themselves to some form of co-operation, especially those which can be carried out over a period of time without any loss in return to the farmers concerned. One example which occurs to me is machinery for clearing out cattle corrals; this is applicable to the west generally, and it is increasingly applicable to eastern areas. Another example is machinery for removing manure piles and distributing them over the fields. This is another job which can be done over an extended period of the year, and it can be done more efficiently by a group which comes in to carry out this particular task than by the farmer himself who is often occupied doing other jobs at a busy time of the year. It does not matter whether it is done in May, June, July or August and it is obviously unwise to have this equipment on only one farm if several farms can share it.
There is another type of operation which comes into this category. It may not be so common in eastern areas but I do know that it is of importance in the Red River valley of Manitoba, namely the harvesting of com and sunflowers. This is an operation which can be carried out over a period of several weeks without any prejudice to the farmer either as to quantity or quality, and it seems sensible that there should be pooled machinery in connection with it. I could outline half a dozen such operations where pooled operations would not only be wise in themselves but where they would not conflict with the ele-
Farm Machinery
ment of human nature which has, in the past, upset so many efforts toward co-operation.
I put this corollary forward because I am trying to demonstrate as best I can that there are arguments in favour of this type of approach. I am also warning the minister and his officials that they can expect trouble with many forms of co-operation in those fields of activity on the farm where everything has to be done at the same time on every farm.
I would like now, if I may, to just put on the record the size of the problem, using figures taken from the d.b.s. handbook. The figures I am going to use are based on the eight-year period from 1954 to 1961. I think they will demonstrate that in this race to get the increased income about which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam was speaking we are barely holding our own, and in some parts of the country we are actually losing ground. I give these figures under two main headings. The first heading is "Realized gross income" and the second is "Operating and depreciation costs".
Any person knowledgeable in farm economics will know that these figures do not include the interest on the land value and the labour of the man working on the land. Let me put these figures on the record to show the house how the race between income and costs is going in Canada. These are national figures and they do not tell the story in regions. I will attempt to clarify that later. In the year 1954 the realized gross income of farmers across Canada was $2.7 billion; the costs were $1.6 billion. I am taking these amounts to the nearest round figure. In 1955 the income was $2.7 billion, and the costs had risen to $1.6 billion plus. In 1956 the income had risen to $2.9 billion plus, and costs had risen to $1.7 billion. In 1957 income was still at $2.9 billion, and the costs were still at $1.7 billion. In 1958 the income jumped rather drastically to $3.1 billion, and the costs had risen to $1.8 billion. In 1959 the income had gone to $3.1 billion plus, and costs had gone to $1.8 billion. In 1960 income had climbed to $3.2 billion, and costs to $1.9 billion. In 1961 income had risen to $3.3 billion, and costs to $2 billion.
These figures show that in the last eight years there has been a rise of 22 per cent in farm income; but the costs during that period have risen 27 per cent. If you take the figures for 1962 and 1963 which are available, you will find this trend has continued. So as a nation, Mr. Chairman, the costs are rising at a greater percentage than the income.

Farm Machinery
When you break it down into farm income per farm-because it must be remembered that not only has farm income been going down and costs have been going up, but the number of farmers has decreased-you get a more accurate picture. In the period 1954 to 1957 the realized gross income, as an average all across Canada, was $4,891 per farm. The operating costs of the average farm in that period were $2,883, leaving a net realized income of $2,008. In the years 1958-1961 the income for those four years was $5,964 per larm; but costs had gone up to $3,514 per farm, leaving a net income of $2,450. If I may do the arithmetic for hon. members, comparing the period 1958-1961 with the four preceding years, farm income had gone up $1,073, costs had gone up $631, and the increase in net income per farm was $443.
Therefore, I think in all fairness we can say that if the federal government is responsible for farm income, there was some betterment of the position; not as much as we would have liked, but at least we reversed the trend that had been there in that first period after the war. So we can say that for each one of those four years the increase in net income, after costs had been taken off, for the average farmer across Canada, was $443 better each year than it had been in the preceding four years. I translated those figures into income per farm to give the real picture and to point out to the committee, and I hope to the country, that progress has been made in meeting this question of farm income. I have given the figures of rising costs to indicate that the battle is still going on and percentagewise the costs are rising, as a nation, faster than the income. If this trend were to continue indefinitely, eventually the net income increase would slow down again and we would be in serious trouble.
When you look at the picture in areas across Canada you get a different story. I broke these figures down for the maritimes, for the same eight years. With regard to the maritimes, if you compare the years 1958-1961 with the previous four years, during those four years the average increase in income per year, per farm, was $431; but the costs went up during that same period each year by $433. By the correction of decimal places it actually works out that in each of those years the average farm in the maritimes lost out by a little better than $1 each year. So in the maritimes, when the rest of Canada was getting ahead by $443 a year income over costs, farmers actually lost $1 a year. I think this gives a very dra-

matic picture of why our attention should be increasingly on the farms in eastern Canada.
With regard to the province of Quebec, once again using the figures per farm, in the four years 1954-1957 the average income per farm was $3,755. It increased in the years 1958-1961 to $4,428. This was an increase of $673 per year, per farm. But the costs during that same time climbed from $2,122 per year, per farm, to $2,767, or a net increase in costs of $645. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, with regard to Quebec farms in those four years the gain of income over costs each year was only $28 per farm, compared to the national average of $443. Therefore Quebec is just barely holding its own, and no more.
With regard to Ontario the figures are a little better. In Ontario the increase per farm, per year, for those four years was $1,173. The increase in costs was $915 per year; so there was a net gain in each of those four years of $258 per farm, as compared to the national average of $443.
The figures in relation to the prairie provinces tell a very dramatic story. Comparing the four years of 1957 to 1961 with the succeeding four years their income increased very dramatically to the extent of $1,315 per farm, and the cost only went up per farm to the extent of $453, which is one of the lowest increases in the whole of Canada. This gives an increase in realized income, when you subtract costs from gross income, of $863 per year per farm. Therefore, western Canada, because it had poured these hundreds of millions of dollars into mechanization, the farmers were gaining the benefits of it, and the gains in income rose quickly over costs as compared to the rest of Canada.
To complete the picture across Canada I will give the figures for the province of British Columbia. The province of British Columbia had an increase per farm for each of those four years over the previous four years of $1,056. Costs went up $748 per farm per year giving a net increase of income of $309 for each of those years as compared to the national average, $443.

I think I can complete my remarks in two or three minutes, Mr. Chairman.
I have put these remarks on the record with the hope that the situation, vis-5-vis

farm income increases, cost increases and realized net income, can be applied to this legislation that the minister has brought in. I know something of the tremendous difficulties that will have to be faced to reduce farm machinery costs, which represent the largest single item of expense in the agricultural industry in Canada today. In eastern Canada of course the highest cost factor is in respect of feed grains.
