speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution which is before this committee is designed to do something about the very serious problems that exist in respect of farm machinery, and how it can best be made available to farmers in view of the heavy costs which are involved. As most members realize, this question of farm machinery, and the high costs which are imposed on farmers, is something which has concerned this House of Commons and the legislatures of some of the provinces for the past 25 years. I think the first committee set up by this parliament was set up in 1937, sat through 1937 and 1938, and made a very exhaustive report to the house, in respect of which unfortunately action was never taken. Other reports have been made, one of the most exhaustive of which was made by a legislative committee of the Saskatchewan legislature. That committee made a series of recommendations, most of which were carried out in so far as they fell within provincial jurisdiction.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle has made reference to the royal commission on rural development in Saskatchewan which sat between 1952 and 1956. He took some time to deal with those recommendations and to offer some criticism in respect of the alleged failure of the government of that province to carry out those recommendations. The hon. member seemed to be somewhat incensed about the fact that I said this afternoon that the real
Farm Machinery
problem facing farmers of Canada today was the lack of farm income. He was only able to belittle this statement by saying he heard me make it 20 years ago. Of course the fact it was made 20 years ago does not destroy it today; it is still true.
As I pointed out in the figures I gave to the house this afternoon, any industry which finds the index price for the things it sells down by 44 points, and the index price for things it buys up by 66 points knows it is on its way to bankruptcy. There are parts of the agricultural economy which do not share this general situation from time to time, but the over-all picture of the agricultural industry is serious, and until we grapple with this problem of farm income we are not going to solve it, and certainly not by putting on little patches. We are playing blind man's buff with this agricultural problem.
The' hon. member for Qu'Appelle dealt with some of the recommendations made by the royal commission on rural development in Saskatchewan, one of which related to nationalization of the farm implement industry and he said, that the reason this had not been done was because socialist governments never believe in socializing anything. I believe that even one as naive as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle knows that one cannot socialize an industry unless it is within one's jurisdiction, and the farm implement industry does not happen to be located in the province of Saskatchewan. The centre of the farm implements manufacturing industry is pretty well located in central Canada, and while distribution is carried on in the province of Saskatchewan and the other prairie provinces, it would be of little value to nationalize distribution when someone else has control of manufacturing. The fact is of course that when the member said this is a field falling within the jurisdiction of the provincial government, and they alone have the power to nationalize the farm implement industry, he is talking complete nonsense. A provincial government could hardly deal with an industry which is nation-wide; but the government of Canada which has power to deal with matters which are for the general advantage of Canada, does have the power to deal with the farm implement industry. The only reason I can imagine why the hon. member for Qu'Appelle spent so much time on this question discussing what happened or did not happen in Saskatchewan is because he was trying to create a smokescreen behind which he could hide the fact that during the years he was federal minister of agriculture noth-

Farm Machinery
ing whatever was done to tackle this problem in respect of farm implement prices. As a matter of fact, a committee of the house was set up and spent I think two years studying this situation, but during at least the last two years the Conservatives were in office the committee was not called together, and the whole thing died after it had received the necessary publicity to create the impression that the Conservatives were concerned about this problem and might eventually do something about it.
Another recommendation of the royal commission on rural development was in respect of co-operative manufacturing and distribution, and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle is quite wrong when he says that was not at all successful. As a matter of fact, Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited has been very successful in its operations.
As a result of loans made to it by the three prairie governments it was able to go into the manufacture in Winnipeg of small farm implements, has been able to enter into long term agreements to buy farm machinery at very acceptable prices from one of the manufacturers in eastern Canada and one in United States; has been able to reduce the price of farm machinery to its members and has brought about very substantial savings for the farmers who make use of the co-operative implements organization. No one should rule out the co-operative manufacturing and distribution of farm machinery as one of the methods for improving the lot of the farmer, in so far as farm implements are concerned.
As a matter of fact, I hope the minister will look into this field, and if the federal government is not prepared at some time to nationalize the farm implements industry it could help by making capital available to the co-operatives so that they could expand their operations both in manufacturing and distribution. I think the competitive effect of a powerful co-operative implement manufacturing and distribution organization in Canada would go a long way toward compelling some of the farm implement companies to get their prices more in line with what they ought to be.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle said that the Saskatchewan government had done something about distribution, but that all it had succeeded in doing was to squeeze some 200 individuals out of business. I make no apology for the kind of people who were squeezed out of business. The government took the recommendation of the royal commission and of a legislative committee and

required all persons who were handling farm implements to be licensed, primarily so that they would be reliable persons who would not only sell machinery but would be prepared to service it and would be prepared to keep on hand adequate supplies of repair parts when they were needed. A farm implement agent has a responsibility to do more than just sell you a piece of machinery and then disappear into the mists. He has a responsibility to be there when the farmer needs a part for his machine, especially if he needs it in the middle of harvesting or when spring seeding is on. He needs to be able to get that part quickly. The licensing was restricted to those who were prepared not only to be financially responsible but to have adequate supplies of parts and repair facilities on hand at all times, and if they were not prepared to stand by the product that they had sold, and prepared to service it and supply parts for it, they could not have a licence.
It seems to me that instead of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle belittling this action he should be commending it, because this is what ought to be done all across Canada. This of course is not a federal responsibility. It is something over which provincial governments alone have jurisdiction. But if people are going to make a very handsome commission, as they do, out of selling farm machinery, then they have a responsibility to stand behind that machinery, to service it and to see that when people want parts for a machine those parts are available. I shall have something more to say about that later.
The other thing which the royal commission recommended, as did the legislative committee, was the setting up of co-operatives for the co-operative use of farm machinery. Again I must take issue with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle who said with regard to these co-operative farms, if I remember the phrase he used, that "failures were legion". I would be obliged if the member for Qu'Appelle would produce figures some time as to the legion that were unsuccessful.
These co-operatives fell into two classes. There were actual co-operative farms, of which I believe 27 were established and I think 26 are still in operation. In the main these farms were set up by veterans when they returned from world war II. They owned the land co-operatively, owned the equipment co-operatively and farmed as a unit. In the main they have been extremely successful. I agree with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that the main problem is a social one rather
than an economic one. Sometimes some of the members did not get along or, more specifically, their wives did not get along, and sometimes they moved off the co-operative farm.
They were generally successful.

But of the less than 30 that were set up I think 26 of 27 or 28 are still operating, and operating most successfully from an economic viewpoint, and I believe from a social viewpoint as well. But the more successful experiment was the setting up of co-operatives for the co-operative use of farm machinery. Between 300 and 400 of these co-operatives were established and they are still in operation. They were particularly designed to help small farmers who found they could not operate with the old horse drawn vehicles and remain in business. Yet if they bought farm machinery their capitalization was greater than the size of their farms warranted.
Not only that, but because their farms were small they bought the smallest kind of machinery, which is the most expensive to operate. A man with a large farm who can buy diesel equipment can purchase fuel at half the price of fuel for an internal combustion tractor. These men who were buying small tractors found that their cost per unit was much higher than that of their neighbour down the road who was using diesel equipment. So these co-operatives enabled groups of farmers to come together, buy large machinery with its low cost of operation and do their farming with this machinery, with the result that none of them had too heavy an investment for the size of his farm and yet was able to get all the advantages of low cost operation.
These co-operatives for the co-operative use of farm machinery have been quite successful. They have had problems, it is true, but they have had a great deal of help from the farm management branch of the University of Saskatchewan. A very careful accounting has been kept of their costs per unit, per acre and per hour, and they have enabled several hundred smaller farmers to remain on the farm and continue operation who otherwise would have been driven off the farm, had they not been able to engage in this type of co-operative endeavour. Therefore when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle says that nothing was done about the royal commission report on rural development, I want to say that everything was done that could be done within provincial jurisdiction, including the matter of licensing, the matter of trying
Farm Machinery
to improve the distribution system, cooperatives for the co-operative use of farm machinery and the co-operative farms themselves.
One other thing was done as a result of this report, which has been most useful. I refer to the setting up of the first and probably the only provincial farm machinery testing operation in Canada. Every piece of farm machinery that comes into the province is tested by a provincial agency set up for that purpose, and the machinery is graded A, B, C, and D and so on. A statement by the agricultural implement engineers accompanies the particular piece of machinery, and at the university and experimental farms it is put under all kinds of tests. A report is written as to its performance, how it stands up under certain conditions and certain strains, and all of this information is made available to the farmers and to the farm organizations. If any farmer wants to buy a piece of machinery in spite of the report, or purchase a piece of machinery that has not been graded, that is his privilege. Nobody can stop a man buying something which has not been proven and about which he knows nothing. But any farmer, before he buys a piece of machinery, can get a report on that piece of machinery. He can find out how it is graded, how it stood up under various types of farming conditions, and before he buys it he knows how it is likely to react under given conditions.
He knows also, when he is dealing with a farm implement agent in the province of Saskatchewan, that the agent must give him a warranty guaranteeing the performance which is advertised. He knows also that the implement agent, in order to retain his licence, must carry repair parts and must service the machinery which he has sold. He must stand by it or take the chance of losing his licence. I say, therefore, that far from decrying the actions which have been taken by the government of Saskatchewan with respect to these reports on farm implements, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, as a member from Saskatchewan, ought to be taking some pride in the fact that there is no province in Canada which has done more, within the limited jurisdiction which a provincial government has, to improve the sale, distribution and servicing of farm implements.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I hope that when we get to second reading of the bill the minister will give us some further information relating to what he has in mind. I am interested in what he calls these farm implement syndicates. Are they to be co-operatives in the

Farm Machinery
true sense of the word, that is will they be organized on the basis of one member one vote? If there is a surplus, will this be distributed on some basis related to the amount of work which is done for each member, or the amount of use which each member makes of the machinery which has been purchased by the syndicate? Will joint stock companies be permitted or will these syndicates be organized entirely on a co-operative basis? 1 hope the minister will tell us whether or not corporation farms are going to come under this type of legislation, because corporation farms are becoming all too prevalent in some parts of Canada. Packing companies and food processing companies have set up farms on which the farmers are paid what is virtually a commission for operating them. Are they going to be able to come under this legislation, or is the legislation designed solely to provide a service for the family farm and the individual farm operator who joins with his neighbours in forming an organization for the purpose of jointly purchasing and using farm implements?
I think there is the germ of an idea here that could be useful, if what the minister has in mind is something similar to the cooperatives for the use of farm machinery. This method could be useful, particularly to the smaller farmers. If this legislation which the minister is going to bring down makes it possible for the smaller farmers to combine themselves so that they can get the advantage of the larger machinery which they cannot afford to own or operate themselves, then it will certainly help to reduce farm costs and do something toward helping get the farmer out of the cost-price squeeze. I want to suggest to the minister that I hope he is not going to accept this as a solution to the problem of farm implement prices. All the investigations which have been made by various royal commissions and parliamentary committees indicate that over the last 30 years, while the labour factor in producing farm implements has reduced on a per dollar cost basis, the amount spent in promotion and advertising has gone up; that a very great part of the excessive cost of farm machinery is due to duplication in the industry and particularly to the duplication of repair services. In every small community there are three or four implement agents, each of whom must carry a supply of repair parts. All of this costs money.
The possibility has been looked into of setting up repair depots at which repair parts for all the different makes of farm machinery CMr. Douglas.]
would be available, rather than having three or four separate agents handling these repair parts in every community. I think the government will have to go much farther. I think the government will have to sit down with the farm organizations in Canada to see if the co-operative manufacture, co-operative distribution and co-operative servicing of farm machinery cannot be worked out, with the government assisting by way of loans to these co-operatives to enable them to set up the necessary factories or to buy out some of the existing farm implement companies. I am convinced that nothing effective will be done about reducing the price of farm machinery to farmers, that nothing effective will be done about removing the costly duplication of services in both the selling and repairing of machinery until the farmers themselves, with whatever assistance the government is prepared to give them, establish effective cooperatives for this purpose. While I hope this measure the minister is introducing will be of some value, and we will know more about that when we get down to examining the legislation, I trust he will not consider this first, faltering step to be a solution to the problem by any means.
For 30 years parliament has looked at this problem, but so far nothing really effective has been done to cope with it. I hope the minister will be prepared, in the not too distant future, to work out a dynamic, bold policy and bring it to this house. I am sure if he does he will have the wholehearted support of the organized farm movement in Canada, and I am sure he will get a good reception from the members of this house.

Mr. Chairman, the resolution that has been introduced today for the purpose of financing what has been termed farm machinery syndicates is certainly a new departure in the provision of farm credit. It is not my intention to embark on a general discussion of agriculture or its credit requirements. Furthermore I do not intend to deal at length with the submissions made by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but I do wish to deal briefly with the remarks made by the minister earlier today.
I was very disappointed at the very brief explanation he gave respecting the application of details envisaged in this measure. I hope he does not misunderstand me; I do not criticize him for being brief, but he ought to be criticised for introducing what could prove to be a very important piece of legislation, what I have already described as a new de-

parture in farm credit, and then failing to give us any of the details of the mechanics of its operation. The only alternative left is to wait until we get the bill and make a detailed examination of it at that time.
The sharing of equipment with others is a well established practice in western Canada. The minister says the intention is to set up a $25 million revolving fund to provide the capital required by the provisions of the bill which this resolution precedes. He also mentioned that it is intended to provide up to 80 per cent of the cost of the machinery purchased by the syndicates that will be established, and one of the obvious deficiencies in the minister's explanation was what he meant by a syndicate.
We have no idea what the requisite terms will be for the incorporation of these syndicates. The minister said they would include three or more farmers; but when we are dealing with legislation to provide a maximum of $75,000 to each syndicate we have a responsibility to protect the public purse in respect of that which is guaranteed by it, in other words to see that we have a reasonable level of security for this extension of credit.
If I may digress for a moment, the minister mentioned the establishment of an interdepartmental board of review for farm credit. We are entitled to a more detailed explanation of this board's functions, of what matters will be referred to it, of what is intended to be reviewed, whether it is the whole field of farm credit, including the Farm Credit Corporation, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, this measure when it becomes law, and whether it will also take into consideration other sources of credit for agriculture available from provincial governments and private concerns?
To return to the resolution, it is fair to say that the sharing of equipment has some historic credence in Canada. I remember many years ago when one, two or three threshing machines took care of the threshing for a whole community. Generally speaking, one tractor and threshing machine were able to look after the needs of 10 to 15 farmers, so it is not a new concept that one piece of equipment will do certain operations for more than one farmer.
When agricultural land was first being settled in the west it was also a rather common practice for large, steam powered breaking equipment to go around communities and do a lot of custom work. Such a piece of equipment was far too heavy and expensive for an individual settler to buy, and in many cases
Farm Machinery
there was almost what one might call a cooperative purchase of such machinery. Also in the case of smaller pieces of equipment, such as crushing and grinding equipment for preparing livestock feed, which was used only a few days a month, or in some cases a few days a week, it was not uncommon for a few farmers to co-operate in the purchase of that equipment.
Mention was made this evening about the possibility of this measure interfering with what is commonly known in the west as custom work, done by those people who make a business of doing work such as seeding or harvesting for so much per acre or so much per hour. I do not believe this legislation ought to be intended to provide credit facilities that would interfere with such a valid, useful and legitimate business.
There is a much more important matter that needs attention, the matter that has been referred to by every previous speaker. It is the matter of equipment costs, and in this connection I am talking about the whole operation of farms in Canada today. Earlier this session we were told by the Minister of Agriculture, and other people also have similar statistics, that in western Canada equipment costs including acquisition, repair and depreciation amount to about 50 per cent of the total operating costs of farming operations in the three western provinces. We should direct our attention to this matter and do something about these tremendous costs of equipment.
We should also bear in mind, so far as custom work is concerned, that finding operators is often as difficult as finding machines at the busy season of the year, and that custom work operators usually have experienced operators who are willing to move on from operation to operation at harvest time.
I do not intend to speak at length this evening, but I wish to say there are several categories of equipment that could usefully be purchased by several farmers, such as heavy trucks used by livestock farmers and grain farmers. For that matter, there are other types of farming operations in western Canada which from time to time require the use of heavy trucks. Trucks are required in the spring for brief periods for hauling seed to be cleaned, ready for planting. They are required at harvest time. They are required to carry stock to market, and so on. But I think it is correct to say that most of these heavy trucks are standing idle in farmers' yards more than 90 per cent of the time. This is

Farm Machinery
one piece of equipment which is very important when you need it. But a farmer does not need it for very long. Thus it seems to me it is a piece of equipment which could properly be purchased under the terms of the bill before us, in spite of the fact that a motor truck is not confined to the category of farm equipment. The minister has not yet indicated whether or not the measure will be limited so as to apply only to certain specific pieces of equipment, but I hope that if this is the case motor trucks will be included in the list.
Perhaps the next most expensive pieces of equipment used on the farms of western Canada-indeed, in some cases they are the most expensive-are grain combines. However there is a problem here, because most of the grain within a community ripens at the same time and some arrangement would have to be worked out among members of a syndicate as to whose crop should be harvested first. Most members from western Canada who are experienced with the problems caused by wet weather at harvest time realize there is always a possibility of differences arising between the members of a syndicate in this regard. I would point out that in the southern region of Alberta this fall, the harvest is already 45 per cent to 50 per cent complete as far as threshing is concerned; a lesser amount as one moves north. If farmers had the services of a heavy combine for a matter of a week it could, on occasion, gather up a grain harvest sufficient to pay for its cost. A few weeks of inclement weather might mean the loss of a whole crop. This would be the problem, though I do not think it is insurmountable: Who would use this equipment first, when weather conditions permit it to be used?
Heavy tillage machinery is another item which no doubt will be considered. In this case, as compared with harvesting, timing is not so delicate and the deterioration or loss of value if the operation cannot be carried out at a particular moment is not so important. Then there are types of equipment designed to handle specialized crops. I think of equipment for harvesting sugar beets, for example. Anyway, if there is to be a specified list of the machinery which can be purchased under this measure I think we are justified in asking the minister to provide such a list. Moreover, he should be willing to accept suggestions for additions. In my own riding and, indeed, throughout southern Alberta there is a need today for a very heavy piece of equipment which could break the prairie, prepare a seed
[Mr. OlsonJ
bed and actually seed tame grass in some of the submarginal land. I do not know whether such a machine is in existence, but it would necessarily have to be a very heavy and costly piece of equipment. One farmer would not have any use for it over an extended period of time; he might want to prepare a few acres of land each year to ensure correct grazing rotation. I bring this up as an example; there are many other specialized pieces of equipment required in connection with other farming operations in various parts of Canada.
In closing, I wish to ask a number of specific questions which I hope the minister will answer, either when he closes this debate on the resolution or when the bill comes up for second reading. First I should like to know what will be the requirements facing these corporations or syndicates. There is clearly some need to protect the guarantees which are to be made by the public purse; a need to see that the machinery will be maintained so that the undepreciated value will always be higher than the unpaid balance of the credit, as well as to make sure that there is some continuity of the syndicate after the money has been expended. Then I should like to know, as I have already indicated, whether the eligible equipment is to be specified. I have already dealt with that point. The third question I should like to ask is this: What are the anticipated terms of repayment? Will the arrangement follow the lines of the Farm Improvement Loans Act or of the administrative provisions applied by the Farm Credit Corporation, with extended terms? Or will there be a variable schedule of repayments to match the estimated depreciation of the machine or machines which have been purchased?
There is another question which I am sure the members of these syndicates will be asking. What security, what personal guarantees will be required from the farmers who form themselves into these groups? This was not dealt with by the minister in his opening observations today. If we could have answers to the questions I have raised I believe we would be in a far better position to discuss intelligently some of the practical applications of this measure as it moves to its further stages.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to put a question to the hon. member who just yielded the floor.

Can he tell us where he has taken his figures, when he mentioned the $75,000 maximum?
All day, I have listened to speeches delivered either by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), or by members, and 1 have not heard of any maximum for such loans.

Is there a special pipeline between the government and the hon. member?
I did not hear the last part of the question.
Is there a special pipeline through which the hon. member receives information from the government, and which we could tap?

I think there were some suggestions in the press during the past weeks mentioning the figure I put forward as a maximum. With regard to the comment about a pipeline, I should like to tell the hon. member that I have enjoyed very good cooperation from the members of the present government as I did from members of the government when his party was in office about a year and a half ago.

Mr. Chairman, my turn has come to make some remarks about the resolution now before us.
The hon. members who spoke before me talked mostly about their respective riding or province; we heard mostly about the western provinces and the usefulness of that resolution for the prairie farmers.
That resolution is meant, as explained by a number of hon. members, to allow some groups of farmers to get together in order to be able, on behalf of their group, to purchase machinery under the new loans which will be granted when the bill which will follow this resolution has been adopted.
However, in the remarks he made this afternoon, the Minister of Agriculture did not say anything which could lead us to believe that in the near future the price of farm machinery would decrease thanks to grants from the federal government or a tax cut, for instance the repeal of the 11 per cent tax which has also affected in its own way the price of farm machinery.
Nothing was said about reducing the cost of farm machinery. But, I recall that in 1949 or 1950, a farmer had to pay from $1,800 to $2,000 for a new tractor, with all the necessary
Farm Machinery
farming attachments. Today, we would pay between $5,000 and $6,000 for such a tractor. It means that the cost of that equipment increased by 300 per cent over the past 15 years.
However, as I have just mentioned, nothing in the act, as it now stands, suggests that the price of farm machinery sold to farmers will be lowered. Instead of lowering prices, we want the farmers, who have to suffer the consequences, to get organized, to form a syndicate or a group of three to buy what one man could afford 15 years ago.
Mr. Chairman, before I took the floor, some hon. members have discussed the practical effects which this resolution will have in their respective riding or province.
We realize, on examining this resolution, that its object was commendable and that those who have prepared it or are encouraging it are surely well intentioned.
But let us look at it in a practical way. It may be practical in some provinces, I have no doubt about that and I am not discussing that point. But as far as agriculture in eastern Canada is concerned, when we come to think of the type of machinery which the farmers will be able to buy through co-operatives under the existing legislation, we realize that this legislation will be almost unworkable in that part of Canada.
Farmers cannot get together to buy a milking machine, for instance, because if they did, they would have to milk their cows at different hours. Perhaps they could manage it but it would go against the cows' nature.
Farmers will not be able to agree either on the purchase of a litter carrier through a syndicate because such a machine is a fixture in the building and therefore, cannot be lent to other farmers.
There are also the hay balers for the storage of hay. Everyone knows, especially in the province of Quebec, that our farmers have been the victims of bad weather for the past few years. When the weather is nice for a few days all the farmers are in a hurry to use their machines to store their hay on time. Consequently, farmers could not get together under this legislation to purchase a single hay baler.
Now, if four or five farmers take advantage of this bill to buy a piece of machinery they will be joint owners and there will be trouble when the time comes to use the machine. On the other hand, when a farmer is the sole owner of a machine he is independent and works when it is convenient; he can make

Farm. Machinery
arrangements with his client as to the day on which he will go and work for him on his farm.
I am looking at the practical side of this legislation. I see that the Minister of Agriculture is laughing. Perhaps it is practical for western Canada to have a combine for five or six farmers, but in the east of the country I certainly cannot see the practical aspect of this measure. I do not deny the good intentions of the minister, but I look forward to reading the bill to be able to say what will be the practical aspect of the proposed legislation.
Can people organize a syndicate in order to buy a tractor? It is impossible. Nowadays a tractor is used daily on our farms. People certainly cannot organize a syndicate to buy one.
Let us analyse our farm situation and see which farm implements we need. The minister should analyse the situation in order to know if it is possible, from the practical viewpoint, to apply such legislation.
I do not deny the good intentions of the Minister of Agriculture, but it would be much wiser and more useful if the minister would introduce as soon as possible measures likely to enable our farmers to get farm machinery at a cheaper cost, so that they might, allowing for the changing weather in the east, do their work at the convenient time.
If five or six farmers are to use the same machinery in eastern Canada, I do not see the practical aspect of such a system.
I think that those who really know the farm problems of Quebec will agree with me when I say that the aim of this resolution is a worthy one, but I am anxious to hear the Minister of Agriculture explain to us the practical side of this legislation.
And now, Mr. Chairman, we are impatiently waiting for this bill to be made available to us.
A lot was said about our farmers' prosperity which is made much of especially at election time. But if today our farmers cannot buy machinery for themselves, they will be able in the future, not because of their prosperous situation but rather because of the farm crisis, to unite to get the machinery which a few years ago each was buying to meet his own needs.

Mr. Chairman, I am delighted with this bill. I was glad to hear the hon. members for Qu'Appelle and Burnaby-Co-quitlam state that they thought it would help somewhat to reduce farm costs. As

the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said, if it helps to reduce these costs a little bit, it will be worth while, and will be well worth supporting. Mr. Chairman, I am not a farmer and so I am no expert in these matters; but I am anxious to see bills of the kind that the resolution speaks of coming before the house, because these are matters which should be of great assistance to those who follow agricultural pursuits in this country. I trust that the bill will greatly assist groups of farmers. The resolution refers to syndicates and I hope this will be of assistance to cooperative movements and, as a result, to the general enhancement of farming in other provinces, in these crucial days for our farming population. Like the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, I trust that this legislation will help the small farmers to band together in order to rise above the cost-price squeeze in the purchasing of equipment.
Mr. Chairman, the purchasing of farm machinery by syndicates composed of farmers is, of course, of assistance to the farm implement business, a business which has been the backbone of industrial life in the city of Brantford, Ontario, over the years. Today in Brantford we have a new farm implement plant which is one of the largest, if not the largest manufacturing plant of its kind in North America. Speaking both for the farming population and for those enterprises engaged in manufacturing of farm equipment, I cannot but be enthusiastic about this resolution. Mr. Chairman, I shall look forward with keen interest to studying the bill.

Mr. Chairman, I have been looking forward to the time when this legislation was presented to the house. I hope the minister will not think this is a complete answer to the agricultural problems of today, because it is not. I should like to point out several things in respect of the cost of farm machinery, of which he may or may not be aware.
First of all I should like to suggest that if as a result of this kind of legislation he thinks he is going to reduce the cost of farm machinery to the individual farmer, he is having a pipe dream. If it has that effect I will be pleased, but I do not think it will. I have some very definite views in respect of how, if he has any desire to do so, he can reduce the cost of farm machinery to farmers all across this country.
Several years ago members of parliament spent a great deal of time accumulating several thousand pages of evidence in respect

of the cost of producing farm machinery. That committee on agriculture, after its detailed study, made certain recommendations, the main one being that the committee should continue to study the problems and look at what was being done by other countries today in relation to the cost of farm machinery.
Mr. Chairman, so far as the resolution and the minister's statement are concerned, I am of the opinion that very little will be done to reduce the cost of farm implements. We have just heard the hon. member for Brantford speak in support of this piece of legislation, and I wonder whether it is going to be more beneficial to the manufacturers of farm machinery than to the farmers. Perhaps that is a good question and one deserving of an answer. Before we accomplish anything in respect of solving the difficulties relating to the cost of farm implements-and I should like to remind the minister that costs incurred by farmers are increasing all the time, while the farm income picture is not rosy- we will have to take more definitive steps than proposed at this time.
We are greatly concerned about what the minister and his cohorts intend to do in respect of rising costs in relation to many farm products including the cost of raising cattle and producing grain, because we are vitally concerned with these difficulties. I suggest one of the ways by which costs incurred by farmers could be reduced is by government leadership in the field of standardization. For the last two or three years I have had a private member's resolution on the order paper in respect of this situation. I believe that if we are going to accomplish anything in this field of standardizing the costs of farm machinery parts we must have leadership from the government. Parts must be standardized before any reduction in costs will be realized, and although there has been a slight step in this direction, we have a long way to go. Farmers complain mainly about the cost of repairs to farm implements. They are familiar with capital costs of machinery, and figure these costs into their over-all plans; but the high and unforeseeable cost of repairs is hurting them badly.
One reason for the high cost of repairs is the lack of standardization in respect of parts. I believe a system of standardization should be set up under the authority of a three man board, one appointed by the farm organizations, one by machine manufacturers and one by the government, and this board could work towards standardization of as many parts as possible. I appreciate that this would involve
Farm Machinery
great difficulties, and that we must continue to maintain private enterprise in the manufacture of farm machinery if we are to keep up to date and make progress in the development of agricultural technology; but we must be able to compete with the rest of the world in agricultural products, if we are to keep this industry healthy, and we certainly should not allow costs of repairing farm machinery to rise out of all proportion. I suggest that the minister give some consideration to my suggestion in respect of standardization when drafting his next bill to assist farmers. This will be difficult, but I think we should make a start by establishing a three man board to look into the situation with a view to gradually bringing farm implement parts under a standardization policy.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam made a suggestion in respect of repair depots. I am not a socialist and do not believe in his theory that we should nationalize the farm machinery industry, and that is what his agriculture minister suggested to the agricultural committee of the Saskatchewan legislature. He suggested that we nationalize the farm machinery industry and do away with private enterprise in this field. I am wondering how the hon. member for Brantford would feel about that sort of proposition put forward by the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam when he was the premier of Saskatchewan.
He might not find it any different having civil servants in the Brantford machine factory.

The hon. member for Timiskaming was also a member of our committee and expressed that same attitude. I intend to also refer to some of the other suggestions made by that committee in respect of the cost of farm machinery.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred also to the fact that labour productivity had increased and that this was not the reason for the increased cost of farm implements. Of course one must realize that one of the conclusions of that committee was that there was a difference of opinion expressed by witnesses in respect of labour productivity compared to the increase in wages. I do not feel competent to deal with the finer economical points of this argument, but there was a considerable difference of opinion expressed by labour unions and management in regard to whether or not the increase in wages could be compared favourably or otherwise to the increase in produc-

Farm Machinery
tivity, or whether in fact increased wages did contribute to the increased cost of farm machinery. I appreciate that the increases in wages were justified and that labour has the right to an improved standard of living, just as do farmers and others, but I do not believe that the nationalization of the farm machinery industry will cut costs incurred by farmers. As I have stated, I think a standardization policy would do much toward that end.
Second, I should like to point out that the majority of farm implements are not manufactured in Canada, unless that factory in Brantford is now engaged in this field. At least in the years 1961 and 1962 there was not one tractor manufactured in Canada. These companies, Massey-Harris, International Harvester, John Deere and Case are international farm machinery companies. They manufacture their machinery in the country where they can find the lowest costs, and they sell their machinery in countries like Canada for what the market will bear, with no regard to their costs. The then general manager of Massey-Ferguson admitted this to the committee when he said in answer to the hon. member for Kent (Ont.) that "market conditions here establish the price of equipment in this market". He went on further to tell us point blank that what they charged farmers in Canada had nothing to do with their costs.
Many years ago the entry of farm machinery into Canada was made available to farmers on a free trade basis, without duty. So we set the stage for these international companies to build their machinery in the country where they could find the lowest standard of living and the lowest labour cost, so that they could then sell their machines in countries like Canada at prices set on the basis of what the market would bear. This is what the general manager of Massey-Ferguson admitted before the committee.
If we really want to do something about the cost of such machinery to the farmers of Canada we have to have regard to the fact that Massey-Ferguson manufactures all its diesel tractors in Coventry, England. If a Canadian farmer wanted to do so he could travel to England and buy an identical tractor from a dealer there for several hundred dollars less than the price for which he could buy it from a Canadian dealer.
Here is the crux of the situation. If we are going to lower the cost of some of this machinery we are going to have to say to these manufacturers that if they want to continue

to enjoy duty free entry of their product into Canada they must sell it to our dealers at a price equivalent to the price at which they sell it to dealers in the country of origin. Our farmers cannot even buy machinery manufactured in the United States from a dealer in Canada at the same price as they could if they went to the United States and bought the same machine from a dealer there. Why is this so? Because our farmers have been suck-ered into a deal where they are paying what the market will bear.
If we want to do something about the cost of farm machinery, let us have a look at the situation which makes it possible for these international companies to operate in this way. Massey-Ferguson puts forward the proposition that they are really a Canadian company because they have their head office here, but most of their manufacturing is done outside of Canada and most of their sales, of course, are also made outside of Canada. These international companies have taken advantage of the free trade situation and in my opinion have in fact conspired to set prices in Canada at what the market will bear. What in fact are Canadian farmers doing? They are paying for the cost of erecting factories in low labour cost countries. If we want to do something about the cost of farm machinery, then let us say to these people that if they are going to bring in tractors from England they must treat their dealers in Canada in the same way as their dealers in the country of origin. If they did so the price of tractors would come down tomorrow by $400 to $500, far more money than the farmers will save as the result of anything contained in this resolution.
I am sure the minister is aware that a year ago the Alberta legislature set up facilities so that farmers could get together in groups to buy farm machinery. This plan has been operating for a year and I believe, subject to correction, that there are seven such groups now operating in the province of Alberta under a similar sort of arrangement to what the minister is now trying to set up. I wonder whether the minister's department has got in touch with the department in Alberta to see how their plan is working. My understanding is that it is working very well for certain types of machinery, but that in the case of harvesting and seeding equipment it does not work very well.
I have spoken to some of those in the group in the Camrose area where they have a farm machinery co-operative and my information is that machinery such as land

levellers, caterpillar tractors and feeding and grinding equipment is ideally suited to this kind of approach but, as a Creditiste member mentioned, what about tractors? A tractor has to be readily available if maximum benefit is to be derived from its use.
If we want to reduce the price of farm machinery we have to do more than is envisaged in this resolution. We have to proceed with a standardization program. I believe we should take the best parts of Saskatchewan's program and institute it on a national basis. I think there should be national standards with regard to warranties because the most common complaint I have had from farmers in my area with regard to farm machinery is not that the dealer would not do anything for them but that the company would not stand behind the warranty. The farmer could not return the machine if he was not happy with it and had nothing but trouble with it. This applies to some of our larger farm machinery companies, even if their head office is in Canada.
These people have had a good market in Canada for their product, and while I appreciate they have provided some jobs in cities such as Brantford, Toronto and Hamilton the number of jobs that the farm machinery companies have really provided have not been that many. Therefore they should think about doing more manufacturing in Canada, particularly in view of the fact that they have had free access to the market here and have set their prices here without regard to their costs. All we say is that our farmers should be able to buy the same tractor for the same price that a farmer has to pay for it in the country of origin, and I am taking into consideration freight and everything else. I know what I am talking about because I had a friend who was going to Scotland price a Massey 35 diesel for me, and if he had purchased it he could have saved $600, even taking into account the cost of shipping the tractor to Canada.
Surely it would be a simple thing for the Minister of Finance to say to these people: You will no longer have free entry into our market unless you show us that you are making this machinery available to our farmers on a basis comparable to that on which you make it available to farmers in the country of origin. This is not restricting trade. This is making sure that these companies do not make suckers of Canadian farmers.
There are one or two other things I wanted to say with regard to the type of machinery
Farm Machinery
that might be worth while under a program such as the minister has outlined. Again I say that this program can be of some little help, particularly with regard to the clearing of land. It seems to me that would be an ideal situation for a group of farmers to get together to buy land clearing machinery, and in my area this is vitally important. I hope the minister will make allowances for this in the bill and that he will not exclude large caterpillar tractors, large breaking plows, large diskers and so on that can be used in clearing and breaking new land, particularly in those areas where there is good arable farm land available.
I also think that the best way to proceed with the bill, once we have it, would be for the minister to refer it to the standing committee on agriculture for its consideration. Many members on this side of the house and some on the other side took part in previous committees which spent some time studying the problem of farm machinery costs. I think the minister should take advantage of their knowledge by submitting the bill to the standing committee on agriculture. I believe that in this way we could hammer out a bill with which we would all be happy and which would be really effective. There have been many questions asked by hon. members who have already spoken. Who is going to qualify? What kind of machinery is going to be available under this legislation? All of these things, of course, so far are merely the subject of conjecture.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat apparently had some word from someone that $75,000 was the amount which would be made available to each syndicate. This is a lot of money, but I can say that in an area such as mine in which clearing and breaking equipment is required, it is not going to be enough. I do not know whether or not the hon. member has a pipe line to the minister's office, but these are some of the problems that could be thrashed out in the committee. Perhaps if the committee were to meet in camera we could hammer out a bill that would be effective, and which would help the farmers right across the country to a greater extent than some superficial bill that will be the subject of so many regulations that it will not be effective. I understand that the farm credit officers are going to administer this measure. If this is correct, then I agree with it. I think this is essential. This is one of the things for which we fought when I pointed out to the minister that he

Farm Machinery
was being pushed around by the justice department in connection with the naming of solicitors.
The idea of having a farm credit officer out in the area is one which we brought about. We think this is a worth-while idea. This is the kind of work such an officer can do, along with his farm credit work. He can supervise some of these applications from these syndicates and find out what they are doing. I feel this is an excellent idea-if it is the idea.
I come back to one other point, and that is the question of regulations. We have to make sure we are not just passing another piece of paper. We have to make sure this is going to work. As I said in connection with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, that measure will not be of assistance if the banks will not lend the money. This type of legislation is fine; it looks good. It will help a few farmers, but I have a suspicion it is going to help the larger farmers who can find $5,000 to go into a syndicate. What is it going to do for the poor little farmer who cannot find $300 or $400 to go into a syndicate which will buy machinery? How is it going to benefit these people?
We will be looking forward with interest to the bill which will be following this resolution. I hope the minister will follow our suggestion that the bill be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, so that we can hammer out a bill which would be a first step toward the effective reduction of farm machinery costs. I hope also he will give consideration to the two areas with which I have been concerned, namely standardization and the importation of equipment from low labour cost countries. According to their own admission, these companies have charged whatever the market would bear. I ask him, along with his colleague the Minister of Justice, to look at whether or not these companies are in fact in breach of the combines legislation in their pricing policies on farm machinery. I refer particularly to machinery which is manufactured in other countries, and this covers the majority of farm machinery now used in Canada. If we really want to do something about the cost of farm machinery, here is an area in which we could save our farmers a great deal of money and in which we may even be able to provide additional jobs by manufacturing machinery in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make about this resolution.
First, I must say that the measure the government is bringing forward today is still but

a pebble in the ditch separating the pitiful income of the farmer from a reasonable income.
I should like to quote what the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) said on television on August 23, 1964:
Never, since 1956, has parliament done so much legislative work in so little time.
Those were the words spoken by the Minister of Justice on August 23 of this year.
On the other hand, on other occasions we have heard the same minister tell us that we were carrying on a filibuster.
Despite all those measures referred to by the Minister of Justice, we have yet to see a concrete one really designed to help the eastern farmer.
For several months we have been hearing about the legislation now before us. Yet, it was put on the order paper only on September 14 last, that is only yesterday. What the minister stated this afternoon does not give us much information on the bill which will be brought forward after the passing of this resolution.
I expected that the minister would give us some information that would enable us to see whether this new legislation would at least put a little stone in the trench separating the farmers' pitiful income from a reasonable revenue.
Now, what would be the maximum amount allowed for that organization or co-operative mentioned in the said resolution? Will it be $75,000? That amount was mentioned by an hon. member a few minutes ago. Will the maximum amount be larger or smaller? We would have liked the minister to tell us.
Moreover, the Minister of Agriculture told us that this agency or co-operative would be made up of three or more members. Now, I wish to point out that in this resolution nowhere is the word farmer used. Maybe it is the intention of the minister, at this time, to eliminate completely this word in future legislation.
As far as I am concerned, even if I am still a farmer, I am not in the least ashamed of it. But it is to be noted that the resolution does not mention that those three persons must be farmers. I think, therefore, that a farm machinery salesman could, for instance, form a syndicate, which would be quite easy for him, for he would only have to ask two other persons, who are farmers, to form this syndicate with him, and after a while, he could sell his share to another farmer. In the meantime he would have sold a lot of farm machinery, and in six or eight months

he could set up the same scheme and form another group or syndicate. As I said before, how are we to know if only farmers or producers of farm products will form such groups.
Now, if such a group is an organization, a co-operative or a syndicate composed of three members, could three brothers who have formed a farm corporation, owning the same farm, the same livestock, organize such a syndicate or co-operative? That is another question I have asked, and I believe that under the circumstances it would serve a good purpose if three members of the same family could form such an organization or syndicate.
Here is another point I immediately thought of when I read the resolution and after hearing the statement of the Minister of Agriculture: What would be the rate of interest charged on loans made to those organizations? Would it be higher than the rate now charged under the Farm Improvement Loans Act or would it be the same as the rate accepted by the present government on loans over $7,500 made under part 3 of the Farm Credit Corporation Act?
Now, what will be the method of reimbursement? Over how many years will the repayment of loans granted to those syndicates be spread? We would have liked the minister to clarify this point when he spoke on the resolution earlier. I think we would have passed through this stage more promptly so that he might ask his officers to make the necessary corrections to the bill and submit it to us afterwards as soon as possible.
There is a further question several of us are asking themselves: Why will this act be administered by the Farm Credit Corporation instead of by chartered banks, as is the case with the Farm Improvement Loans Act?
I approve the Department of Agriculture for having entrusted the implementation of this measure, the provisions of which I do not know yet, to the Canadian Farm Credit Corporation, because I know several advisers of this corporation and I am aware of their wide experience in the preparation of such loans, and I am convinced that they will be able, by working in agreement with their advisers throughout all the provinces, to deal with this measure which is highly prized by the farmers; they have, in many areas, efficient advisers who will be able to welcome and advise the farmers who are anxious to set up syndicates.
Farm Machinery
I should like to take this opportunity to say to the minister that it is very nice, indeed, to introduce pieces of legislation to enable farmers to purchase farm machinery, but it is even more important to be able to advise farmers in such a way that they will not engage in a series of commercial operations they may be sorry for in a few months or years. If, in a given area, the farm counsellor takes time to pay the necessary attention to farmers who want to unite in a group and to give them appropriate advice by explaining to them the best way to organize themselves, I think the Farm Credit Corporation will play a part which will be beneficial to all farmers in this country.
When a group of farmers wish to form a syndicate or a co-operative to buy machinery, they must necessarily know the operating cost per hour of work of a combine for instance. I am unable to tell you what it is, but the farmer must know. If the Farm Credit Corporation has those figures, the farmers can meet its farming counsellors and establish their program before buying machinery they would then know the annual rate of depreciation, the interest charges and the method of reimbursment, and they could make their purchase accordingly.
I know that we will resume consideration of all these questions when we study the bill.
But before reading the bill I should like the Minister of Agriculture to give me a few answers, so that I will not have to move amendments to this bill when it is brought before us.
As the hon. member who spoke before me said a moment ago, it would have been preferable for this bill to be submitted to the committee on agriculture and colonization, so that every member informed by the advice of officials of the department could express his idea in order to hammer out the best possible legislation.

Mr. Chairman, no matter has come before the House of Commons of as much importance to the agricultural industry as that of the cost of farm machinery. About six months ago I listened to the minister addressing the municipal convention in Regina. I recall the plateau he was on at that time, and the forecast he made of the inroads that would be made into the problem of farm machinery costs, and his forecast of what the government would do to attack that problem. If this resolution is the result of all the intervening months' work, then I for one am sincerely disappointed.

Farm Machinery
When I say that, I do not intend to indicate that this is a useless measure in itself; but if it is the sum total of all those months of study, and of the long hard look that was taken at this problem, then it is a weak and pale measure indeed.
The hon. member for Shefford indicated his belief that this would be a more useful measure for farmers in western Canada than for those in other parts of the country. I am inclined to agree with him. In fact I am inclined to go a little further and say it will be of more benefit to the larger farmer than to the smaller farmer who, for the past several years, has been the chief concern of governments both at the provincial and federal level. I am interested in this word "syndicate". I wonder why it is used in this resolution, and whether it will be used in the bill. I wonder whether this measure envisages the setting up of simple co-operatives for the purchase of machinery they require. If this is so, why does the minister not want to use the word accepted in most farm communities across Canada, rather than the word "syndicate" which is before us at the present time.
There is one other question I should like to raise. In the last several months, particularly the last five or six months, the Minister of Agriculture has indicated a desire to get the provinces to bring in legislation supplementary to the legislation he proposes-legislation which, I take it, is encompassed by the measure now before us. I should like the minister to tell us whether he has been successful in securing commitments or indications from any of the provinces that they are willing to bring in legislation which will complement or supplement the legislation envisaged in the resolution before us.
I think back to the inquiry into the cost of farm machinery which was undertaken by the government several years ago, when we were sitting on the other side of the house. I recall the frustration some of the members of that committee felt as they questioned the officials of certain of the companies which came before the committee at that time. One member who spoke today in the debate said we took no action on the recommendations of that committee during the last few months during which we were in office. I cannot allow that observation to pass without making reference to the determined obstruction mounted by members opposite, who then formed the official opposition, obstruction which prevented the government from completing many of the courses upon which it bad embarked in its first years of office.

I know the minister is a learned man in many ways and that he keeps in close touch with what is happening in the business world in Canada. I suggest he take a look at what has happened to the value of Massey-Harris shares in the last few years. This will give him some indication whether or not an inquiry into the cost of farm machinery should now be undertaken for a second time, and proceeded with. No one can deny that the situation has changed, even since the inquiry which was held some two years ago.
The fact that these arrangements are to be under the supervision of the Farm Credit Corporation brings up the question of the interest rates to be charged on these loans to farmers. I want to tell the government that if in the bill they propose to bring before parliament there is a further erosion of the principle which was embodied in the Farm Improvement Loans Act as it existed before the present administration came to office, this will be another step along the road which will raise instead of lowering the cost of loans to farmers across this country. I notice that certain people have been taking notes, and I hope the minister and his officials will take note of that observation. I trust we shall not have to rise when the bill is brought forward and oppose it on that ground, at least.
Another matter which was mentioned briefly by an earlier speaker this evening concerned the nature of the syndicates or cooperatives themselves. As I mentioned, in western Canada Canadian Co-operative Implements Limited has been operating for some years. This organization was set up in an attempt to reduce the cost of farm implements, and it is a fact that in the past two years dividends from the company have amounted to between 10 and 12 per cent. This immediately raises the question as to the nature of the syndicate or co-operative or other form of company which would be set up to make possible the purchase of machinery in accordance with the provisions of the bill to be laid before us. Dividends will be forthcoming to the purchasers, and there must be some basis upon which these dividends can become the equity of those to whom they belong.
Another problem which concerns farmers in this regard has to do with warranties, and this too has been mentioned by an earlier speaker. In Saskatchewan I believe the leader of the New Democratic party indicated his belief that the problem had been licked or, at any rate, that an effort had been made to solve it. I can assure the committee that

this is far from the truth. Farmers on the prairies today are having a difficult time with the implement companies as far as warranties are concerned. Many of the machines coming off the assembly lines now are not proven. But farmers who find them unsuitable for the operations for which these machines were purchased are often unable to return them to the manufacturers when it is apparent they are not performing satisfactorily.
A word now about parts. As I recall it, when the inquiry into the cost of farm implements was under way the implement companies presented what seemed to many of us a very fair case with regard to the parts carried for the farm people. But this still remains one of the problems facing those who buy machinery-the fact that parts of many of these machines are not as readily available as they should be, even for new machines. This is particularly damaging when a replacement part is needed at seeding time, or during the harvest or in the course of some other urgent farm operation.
I am disappointed in this resolution and in its terms. If this is supposed to be the answer the government has to the high price of farm machinery I can only say it is a poor substitute indeed for legislation which could have accomplished its purpose more effectively. It will help only a limited number of people, in many cases people who would otherwise be able to secure the credit they need from other sources-and I am not referring to those sources which are charging 12, 14 and 16 per cent. I know the minister has been anxious to create the impression that he intends to do something for agriculture. We on this side like to think he is sincere in that desire. But when I look at this resolution I cannot see very much in it which will enhance the prospects of the agricultural community of Canada. In so far as agriculture is concerned, it is one of the weakest resolutions that has ever been brought before the parliament of this nation, when one compares its limited extent with the promises that were held out, almost on a daily basis, from one end of this country to the other by the Minister of Agriculture. In view of this, sir, all I can say is that if the bill follows the terms of this resolution, it will be a shocking dereliction of duty, in so far as the promises that were made to the farmers across this country are concerned.
I say that it is particularly shocking to those in eastern and central Canada, and the smaller farmers in other parts of Canada,
Farm Machinery
who will find this legislation almost useless to them in their struggle to beat the cost-price squeeze that today engages the attention of farmers across this country. I am sure the minister and his officials have been taking notes during this discussion, and perhaps this point has occurred to them already; but I would hope that grain handling,, grain storage and grain cleaning equipment would also be included in the definition of "farm machinery" when the definition is decided upon. I do not think I have anything, else to say at this time, Mr. Chairman, except that I hope the bill is much better than the resolution would indicate.

Mr. Chairman, I and many other members of this house have been greatly interested in this proposed piece of legislation, perhaps because the minister has gone across the country talking about it and saying what it would do to the agricultural economy. I think at one time he said it. would revolutionize the agricultural economy of this country. We have been waiting anxiously for this measure to be introduced, f have a brief clipping from a Lethbridge newspaper away back in April, when the minister made a statement in Lethbridge and said, "Farmers, wait". Well, Mr. Chairman,, this house has been waiting since that time, and at last this measure is on the order paper and is before us.
In Lethbridge in the spring the minister said he could not supply any information with regard to what he envisaged would be in the bill, and he did very little better when introducing it at the resolution stage. He failed to enunciate what he meant by the word "syndicate". An hon. member asked,. "Does it mean three farmers or more? Can it be two farmers and their sons who are already operating farms?" We really do not know. What does it apply to; what does the minister mean by the words "farm machinery"?
I can remember that a couple of years back I had quite an interesting discussion about the terms "farm implements" and "farm machinery". What do these terms include? I could ask, for example, will they include feed mills, and a syndicate opening and starting to operate a feed mill for the purpose of feeding their own livestock? Will it cover those people who are going to be in the business of dealing with livestock or buying livestock? I hope the minister will consider these points before bringing in the bill. The resolution says:

Farm Machinery
-the terms and conditions of such loans, the amount of a loan not to exceed 80 per cent of the actual price to the farm machinery syndicate-
What does the minister mean by "farm machinery"? Does he mean that the provisions of the bill will apply only to machinery, and not to livestock? Certainly anybody in the feeding business knows that he can put his own money into livestock and put the government's money into the feed mills, corrals, and the feed distribution system, which has become highly automated in the last five years in particular.
Perhaps the most one can say for this resolution, as it has been devised by the minister, is that it is his hope of doing something for the farmers. But whom will it help? Will it help the grocery growers, the food manufacturers, or just the plain farmer? Will it help the wealthy farmers, or will it help those who need help the most?
Some years ago when we were on the other side of the house we implemented the Farm Credit Corporation, or revised the old farm loan board. It was a well established fact that the old farm loan board only helped those who did not really need it, who had financial backing to help themselves. We established the Farm Credit Corporation under the principle of helping those who needed help; in fact, one who had already established himself on an economic unit could not obtain a loan from the Farm Credit Corporation. During this session quite recently we saw some erosion of this principle; we saw the Farm Credit Corporation granting loans up to $40,000 and $55,000, when it was a well established fact that anybody obtaining a loan of $40,000 from that corporation should at least have collateral equalling $40,000.
Now we have before us a proposal that is going to be operated by the Farm Credit Corporation, and the provisions of the bill will mean that loans will be granted to syndicates. I do not know what the minister thinks of farmers. From his definition, or his evasion with regard to the word "farmer" I am led to believe that he has perhaps been ashamed of being called a farmer all his life, and has been trying to find a new name for himself. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I am not ashamed of the name "farmer" and I have always been proud to be proclaimed as one. But the Farm Credit Corporation was set up with the basic principle of helping those who needed help most. Now, however, we find that the Farm Credit Corporation is helping those who need it the least. Certainly any farmer, or any ten farmers in

any part of Canada would not like to be called grocery growers and would hate to be called a syndicate. I am sure farmers would view that title with some scepticism, to say the least. In this resolution we fail to see any definition of the words "farmer" or "syndicate". Would it include a lawyer, for example, who is practising a law business but also operates a farm on the edge of town? Would this measure allow him to go into the feeding business, for example? This is, of course, occurring in many areas of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it 10.30?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if the committee had a disposition to give this bill first reading tonight-and I sense that it has- we might be disposed not to see the clock and let the hon. gentleman complete his interesting remarks. In that event, we might give the bill first reading.

Mr. Chairman, I think it might facilitate the speed with which the house deals with this measure at the resolution stage if we could get some answer from the government as to whether this brand new legislation will go before the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. That committee is not holding any meetings now and would be free to give this legislation a detailed examination outside the house, and therefore the house could go on with other business.

Mr. Chairman, we have given this bill a great deal of consideration. We realize that after the bill has been in operation for possibly a year some parts of it will perhaps need amending. But it is important, I think, in so far as farmers are concerned, and I believe that after hon. members of the committee see the bill they will agree with this. I have listened very carefully to all the questions that have been asked this evening, and I think they are all answered in the bill. I do not think one question has been asked that is not answered by one of the clauses of this bill. Mr. Chairman, I also should indicate that I have discussed this proposed legislation with all of the ministers of agriculture of the ten provinces of Canada, and they have indicated they think this is an excellent bill.
Who do you say thinks this is an excellent bill?

I have discussed it with all ten of the provincial ministers of agriculture of Canada, and they agree with me that there

are no specific items of machinery not covered, or that will not be covered by the legislation. Be that as it may, I think we could go ahead and accept the resolution tonight, then have the bill presented, which I am sure is selfexplanatory.
Mr. Chairman, I intend to continue my remarks or call it ten thirty.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is my suggestion that we allow the hon. member to complete his remarks so that we might be in a position then to give the bill first reading. In view of the importance of this legislation I am sure all hon. members are interested in seeing the bill, so as to be in a position to discuss it more thoroughly at the second reading stage.

Mr. Chairman, there is little value in doing that unless we know this is the last speaker. There may be other speakers, and by sitting for an extra 20 minutes or half an hour only to find that there are others would be useless.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if I am not too
much out of order perhaps I could ask the members of the opposition parties present whether there are any others who intend to speak at this stage, and if there is an indication that this is the last speaker I am sure we would all be interested in listening to him so that we may receive this bill and make some real headway.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether there are any other speakers to follow me, but I do know I have ten or twenty minutes left which I intend to use, and if the committee is good enough to stay and listen to me I will complete my remarks. I might say that I asked for permission during the flag debate to speak longer than my allotted time and it was not given. Those members on the opposite side seem to have had a change of heart. I will gladly forgo my further remarks at this time if the minister will state that this whole question in respect of farm machinery will be referred to the agriculture committee, and that representatives of farm organizations, machine companies and other interested parties will be heard, so that we will have a better idea of what is envisaged by this legislation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the house leader whether we are to carry on tomorrow with the two resolutions now in front of us?

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will carry on with the business as announced yesterday and try to complete-I hope we will-the resolution stage of the farm machinery syndicate bill. I might try to communicate with the house leaders to find out whether it would not be possible to complete the other stages of that bill tomorrow. I am not prejudging any issue, of course. I say that, in view of the importance of the measure as already stated by the Leader of the Opposition.
We will then take the resolution preceding the crop insurance bill, to be followed by the continuation of the debate at the committee stage of the redistribution bill. I should like to say that beginning Thursday, as announced, we will be taking estimates. The order will be that already announced, that is the Department of Transport to be followed by northern affairs, public works and citizenship and immigration.
